The course of time rolls on; the autumn is chilling. In the great forest, the leaves fall; the precarious green turns to crimson. As the years grow old, one treads upon the frost.

Startled, he was moved to deep reflection; he shut his room to avoid the wind, yet his grief remained as if his ears were stuffed with wax. Suddenly, a brisk breeze arose and the myriad apertures of nature roared in protest.
In this moment, he attained a sudden realization regarding what he had previously heard: the Buddhas of the three periods of time are merely messengers who transmit words.

By touching upon these categories and extending his understanding to all things, he comprehended their underlying meaning. "What does Heaven say? It speaks of nothing, yet within the vast emptiness of space, it spontaneously gives rise to the natural music of the universe.

Regarding the sounds of the human reed-pipes and the earth-reed pipes, what has the Buddha said? For no other reason than this, within the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, he expounded the teachings on the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
these are all transmitted words. Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-karaṇīya-hetu-pratyaya*):
to point directly to the human mind, to see one's nature and thereby become a Buddha. He spoke spontaneously from his mouth the three vehicles and the ten...
The two divisions of the Teaching comprise five thousand and forty-eight fascicles, constituting the entire Great Canon (*Tripitaka*). There is not a single dharma that can be spoken;

this is like the transmission of words through the natural resonance of the heavens (*tāilèi*). Yet, as the various Bodhisattvas differ in the levels of their stages and the depth of their realization, the Vehicle manifests expedient means, providing protection, mindfulness, and entrustment.
Whether through the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, beings are guided according to their capacities so that their measure may be fulfilled and their vows realized.
And so it ends. Although they claim to point directly, they have already become circuitous. This is like the "earth-whistles," the voices transmitted through the myriad apertures.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, among those who interpret the meaning of the teachings, each person had their own master, and each master had their own doctrine.

The *Āgama*, *Vaipulya*, *Pratyekabuddha*, and *Bodhisattva* were categorized as the four teachings; schools were established with distinct gates, and everyone opened their mouths to clamor in contention. This is like the "human whistles," which consist of the various bamboo flutes.
This is a transmission of the words. Since the invention of the flute, the natural resonance of the heavens can no longer be heard.

This *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was spoken by the Buddha and Subhūti within the field of Prajñā; their voices met like the simultaneous snapping of beaks, with golden needles perfectly harmonizing.
Speaking directly and then speaking in reverse, they turned it over again and again without ceasing, yet there was no discrepancy between them. One word was spoken, then repeated once more.

He spoke at length without ceasing, yet it was not tedious; he affirmed without affirming, denied without denying, and accepted without accepting. He established his sweeping arguments without end, yet they were not fragmented;
sometimes he suppressed, sometimes he elevated, sometimes he confirmed, and sometimes he refuted. His exchanges and responses continued without pause, yet they did not become diffuse.
Is it not all due to causes? It is because the capacities of sentient beings vary in superiority and inferiority, and the cultivation of the Bodhisattvas varies in suddenness and gradualness.
Thus, the teachings bestowed are either direct pointing or indirect completion, skillfully guiding according to conditions.

This is like the natural resonance of the wind blowing through myriad things differently, which harmonizes with the various apertures of the earth’s resonance, allowing each thing its own nature and causing them all to take what they themselves receive. The Buddhas of the three periods...

The Buddha. It is for this reason that he is called the "Messenger of Truth. Being old and weary with illness, I have read these words with my eyes and contemplated them with my mind until I attained some realization.
Thus, relying upon the scriptural texts and summarizing their essential meaning, I have composed this "Direct Exposition" to show to my disciples.
I do not dare to merely mimic the conventional sounds of flutes; for if one does not speak directly, the Way will not be seen. I shall therefore speak directly.
General Principles, Rule Six:
According to the title of the scripture, it is called *Vajra*, which signifies Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). The *vajra* is the king of all jewels; it is most firm and most sharp.
When the world is destroyed, the seven treasures are all destroyed, but the secret treasury of the nature-jewel (*prakṛti-vajra-ratna*) cannot be broken.
It is destroyed. Yet this sutra is the king of the Dharma-treasures; the Buddha-nature resides within it.
When the vessel-world (the physical universe) is destroyed, the sutra and the Buddha-nature remain ever-present within the Dharma-store, likewise firm and indestructible.

The commentator [of this sutra] lacks knowledge of the Buddha-nature, yet claims to discourse upon the Buddha-dharma. As for the reader, their own inherent Buddha-nature is neither one nor two. It is not...
One may merely grasp the meaning through words alone; this is said to correspond only slightly with the essential intent (*tātparya*) of the *Vajra*.

According to this sutra, the ancient edition was divided into thirty-two sections, each with its own title. This initial practice of such division originated with Prince Zhaoming of the Liang dynasty.
Although the resulting karmic retribution for this act has now been experienced, later commentators failed to delete these divisions, and thus the number of sections remains.
This [previous version] was fragmented; the intent of the sūtra was interrupted, the logic and phrasing were mutually contradictory, and there was no continuity whatsoever in its structure.
This was not the Buddha’s intention. Now, in this commentary, I dare not follow such an example, but instead rectify the previous errors by unifying the sūtra into a single chapter.
I have endeavored to ensure that the questions and answers correspond clearly and that the underlying insights are harmoniously integrated.

At the points where the discourse unfolds or concludes, I have briefly demarcated sections so that those who take up the brush may find it convenient for their annotations, and those who read the scripture may find it easy to focus their attention.
According to this sutra, the old edition was divided into two volumes, upper and lower.

Following the previous division, the first fourteen sections constitute the upper volume, and from the fifteenth section onward constitutes the lower volume; the Tripitaka edition followed this precedent.

This was inherited from the preceding texts for the convenience of binding and cataloging, and thus people practiced it without noticing the discrepancy. In my humble opinion, if a division into volumes is required, it should follow the [actual] sutra.
From the beginning up to "the retribution of the fruit is also inconceivable" constitutes one fascicle.
From where Subhūti again requests [the teaching on] "abiding the mind and subduing the mind" until the end constitutes two fascicles; this is highly appropriate in terms of its meaning.

For the establishment of the doctrine within the sutra, the former is taught for Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained realization, while the latter is taught for Bodhisattvas who have already attained realization. The former is shallow; the latter is profound.
The latter part is profound; it does not obstruct the flow of the sutra’s logic. This lacuna awaits a future scholar to resolve.
According to the textual structure of this scripture, it should constitute a single fascicle rather than being divided into multiple sections or fascicles.

This approach is seen only in the modern-day Master Han (Zhang Zhongfu), who established a unique precedent. However, regarding the way he connects the paragraphs within the scripture, there are points that cannot be left unchallenged.
The present commentary largely follows the established text of Master Han (Zhuhong), with minor differences in its divisions.

Examining the commentaries on this sutra by various schools, one finds they are not uniform; upon careful scrutiny of their exegesis, they cannot avoid mutual contradictions and rarely achieve a comprehensive synthesis.
Frequently, questions and answers are redundant and the sequence is disordered, such that the reader easily becomes overwhelmed, like gazing out at the vast ocean.

In his *Deciding Doubts* (*Jueyi*), the modern Master Han (Hanshan Deqing) set aside the preceding text and offered a distinct interpretation. Opening the volume, one finds it brilliantly illuminated;

upon a single reading, everything becomes clear and penetrating. My humble opinion is that since an interpretation arises from the presence of doubt, one ought first to raise the doubt and only then resolve it.

To present the state of doubt in advance before Vimalakīrti has even asked his question seems somewhat inappropriate. In this current commentary, I follow Han’s version for the most part, extracting the scriptural passages from both the preceding and following sections.
Continuing on, they are linked together without interruption, forming a single chapter of the sutra. This seems not to greatly contradict the Buddha’s mind.
Those with discernment have instructed me:

according to this sutra, it is not the word of a single school; the masters of the various schools proclaim their own tenets, while the teachers of the doctrinal systems cite their respective scriptural characteristics. Each...
I have set forth what I have perceived and laid bare the ancestral tradition. Yet, even in my investigation of the adamantine ultimate truth, there remains one layer yet to be penetrated.

My present commentary does not reach the level of the Patriarchal Words (*zongyu*) nor does it engage with the scriptural teachings (*jiaocheng*); its sole purpose is to accord with the Buddha-mind and point directly to the realization of one's nature.

Throughout the commentary, where I occasionally cite the scriptures or the teachings to provide supporting evidence, this is likewise an interpretation intended to join the tracks of the same carriage.
The Essential Theme of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra:
Every sūtra must have its own essential theme. As for this *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it should...
Taking "signlessness" (*animitta*) as its central tenet, the sutra proclaims that there are fourteen instances where the so-called "four-line verse" appears.
It definitively identifies these as being free from the mark of self (*ātman*), the mark of a person (*pudgala*), the mark of a sentient being (*sattva*), and the mark of a life-span (*jīva*).

These four lines constitute the essential purport of the entire sutra. Yet, the commentaries of various schools have for the most part fallen into vague generalities; throughout the successive dynasties, the [orthodox] lineage...

The Master does not wish to bestow the true Dharma upon others; he mostly draws from the "upward phrase" and the "final phrase" to proclaim the fundamental principles of the school, refusing to explain them fully.
He causes beginning practitioners of Chan to grope in the void, leading them to investigate the four-line verse within their own very being.
Only when they have reached the point where the mountain ends and the water runs dry will the adamantine mind suddenly open wide.
The eye emits the true light of *prajñā*. This original four-line verse is my own fundamental face;

it is devoid of the marks of self, person, sentient being, or life-span. Whether the entire *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* explains horizontally or vertically, whether it speaks provisionally or ultimately, it is nothing other than a desire for people to empty themselves of these four marks and return to their own portion of *prajñā*. I...
The various marks of persons, sentient beings, living souls, and life-spanners are like grasping at the moon in water or seeking one's own head in a mirror;

they are utterly unobtainable. Therefore, on that day, when the Bodhisattva Maitreya ascended to the Tuṣita Heaven and requested instruction from Maitreya regarding what constitutes the four-line verse, Maitreya said:
"There is no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of sentient being, and no mark of life-spanner."
This is precisely that mark. This is the intimate and compassionate heart of Maitreya; he has spoken it through, breaking open the seal with a single word.
Later, the Great Master Huineng took the Mahāprajñāpāramitā as the truth. Fu Dashi said:
"If one discusses the four-line gāthā, it should not be separate from the mind. Thus, the myriad words and phrases of the sages of antiquity all point to this.
It is not that he does not wish for people to directly take responsibility and recognize the True Teaching of formlessness;
thus, the entire *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* would suddenly become redundant words. Subsequent commentaries on the sutra have not been of a single school:

some have taken the four lines on "seeing with form or seeking through sound" as a verse, while others have taken the four lines on "dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows" as a verse. None of these are incorrect; one should know this.
The two verses in the sutra state that those who have not transcended desire must abandon the marks of form (*rūpa*).

Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), it is the grasping of the markless mark (*animitta-nimitta*) that is real, while the mark of having marks is but an illusion. To examine this sutra minutely:
one sutra is like one part; one part is like one verse; one verse is like one word. Now tell me, from where does this single word arise?
Where does one find the commentary? In days of yore, whenever Master Zhaozhou encountered a student entering his room, he would have them take the "Mu" (無) character as their *huatou*.
This single "Mu" encompasses heaven and earth and manifests the myriad phenomena of the universe.
Only by recognizing the essential principle of the Vajra School can one truly engage in the practice of Chan and awaken to the Way; only then will there be even a slight degree of resonance.

The purport of this teaching, the general meaning of this sutra, is specifically intended for noble beings of the first stage— great-minded Bodhisattvas, whether they have already awakened or not— who,
while practicing with attachment to signs, fail to realize the signless fundamental essence. It is not intended for all ordinary people or outsiders whose minds are deluded.
This is due to the presence of false views. A sutra states: "The Tathāgata speaks for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna; he speaks for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.
These two types of noble beings are truly not comparable to ordinary people, as they have already resolved their great Bodhicitta within the Mahāyāna and the Supreme Vehicle.

Yet, it is regrettable that they have not yet been able to completely forget the dual attachments to persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi* and *dharma-dṛṣṭi*), nor have the four marks [of self] been...
"Empty. These three minds have not yet been fully understood; they have not yet been subdued, nor is their place of abiding known.
Even if one knew their place of abiding, one would still be unable to avoid dwelling in a single location, and thus could not give rise to the mind while dwelling nowhere.
Out of compassion, the World-Honored One preached this sutra, first causing Subhūti to pose the question, with the assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples present."
In meditative concentration, he was like Kāśyapa; in extensive learning, he was like Ānanda; in supernormal powers and wisdom, he was foremost in preaching the Dharma.
That all the noble and holy Sangha did not grant him [this rank] was because this sutra was specifically composed for the purpose of elucidating emptiness.
The noble ones of the first stage and bodhisattvas of great resolve have not yet attained the "passing of the heart through emptiness" (*xin kong qi di*).
Consequently, they often pursue outwardly. Among them, the most superior take the salvation of sentient beings as their daily concern;

they resolutely desire to lead all living beings throughout the entire earth to Buddhahood before they themselves cease. With diligent and unwavering effort, they tirelessly exhort and awaken others, knowing nothing else but this.
The one who can deliver belongs to the self; those who are delivered belong to others.

All sentient beings and all their merit and lifespan arise from the dualistic views of "self" and "others. When the Buddha preached this sutra, he first began with the theme of delivering sentient beings.

This is because sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu* have not yet been fully delivered; therefore, all sentient beings of self-nature are brought to extinction through *nirvāṇa without remainder*.
This is gathered into the four-line verse, where everything is resolved once and for all.
Thus it is said: "There are no sentient beings who attain extinction. To subdue the mind and cause it to abide—nothing precedes this. The mind.
Once one has "dwelt," one cannot avoid dwelling in a single place; this arises from the views of sentient beings.

Whether it be seeking blessings through giving, seeking blessings through prostration and making offerings, or seeking blessings by adorning Buddha-lands—all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are nothing other than practices attached to signs (*nimitta*).
It is not as real as upholding even a four-line verse, which is the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, those who dwell in a single place may realize cause and effect, cultivate the six perfections, or open the five eyes, appearing as though they have something real upon which to rely;
yet ultimately, they do not equal our Buddha, the World-Honored One.

In the past, at the assembly of Dīpaṃkara, he personally received the prediction of enlightenment, yet regarding the Dharma, he truly attained nothing. Only upon reaching this stage can one be called a "Fourfold One" (Caturvidha).

The marks are entirely empty, adorned with myriad virtues. When one regards those various acts of giving, various offerings, various forms of reverence, and various establishments for cultivating merit, they are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, dew, and lightning.
Therefore it is said: "It is taught for those who set out upon the Mahāyāna; it is taught for those who set out upon the Supreme Vehicle."
If one preaches for the sake of sentient beings, then one inevitably teaches them to practice giving, to make offerings, and to worship and adorn stupas and temples in order to seek karmic rewards.
The Dharma gates of the four fruits, the six perfections, and the five eyes are not within the realm of such people;
there is no need to laboriously establish or sweep [for them].

The title of the sutra expresses its meaning through the term "Vajra. In the Western Regions (India), there exists the Vajra jewel, which is exceedingly firm and sharp, indestructible, yet capable of destroying all other things;
therefore, this is taken as a metaphor for the true wisdom of Prajñā. It remains unbroken throughout kalpas...
It destroys; it is able to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*). Vajra is the essence (*tattva*) of Prajñā, while Prajñā is the function (*vṛtti*) of Vajra.
Essence and function are unified, and both converge in the same destination, which is called "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*). That other shore is the ground of awakening (*bodhibhūmi*);
this shore is the ford of delusion. Sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of suffering, trapped in the current of birth and death, unable to [emerge] on their own.
Crossing Over. The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā is like a life-preserver for crossing the ocean or a raft for navigating midstream; by relying upon it, one attains deliverance.
When the Buddha preached this sutra, he intended for people to empty themselves of the four marks (*catur-nimitta*):
there is no self that can cross over, no person who is crossed over, no sentient beings or life-spanners on this shore, and no blissful land or city of merit on the other shore. One.

The Great Canon does not depart from this meaning; therefore it is said: "Sūtra" means "path. It is the path that directly points to the human mind for the realization of one's nature and the attainment of Buddhahood.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Then, at the time for eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having gone through the city begging for alms in due order, he returned to his original place and ate his meal.
Having finished, he gathered his robe and bowl, washed his feet, spread out his seat, and sat down.
First, he set forth what he had heard; second, he set forth the time; third, he set forth the principal figure; fourth, he set forth the location; fifth, he set forth the assembly.
Then, from the perspective of the principal figure’s position, he detailed the ordinary daily activities of putting on robes, eating meals, walking, and staying.
Sitting and reclining, all emerge in succession from the light of Prajñā. The four marks dissolve and return to the markless;

this is attained through quiet contemplation. According to the scriptural text of the subsequent dialogue, the Buddha and Subhūti were like a hen and her chick pecking and hatching simultaneously, their eyebrows knitted together.
The four marks are equalized as they silently realize the principle of the markless. It is as if he asked before he had even been answered.
Sometimes he answers before being asked; sometimes he answers according to the question; sometimes he answers as soon as the question is posed; sometimes he departs from both question and answer;
and sometimes he is neither questioning nor answering. In total, this constitutes one period of establishing [the teaching] and one period of sweeping away [delusions].

It is like a needle meeting its eye or water blending with milk. To speak of it through parables is not to be diffuse; to speak of it repeatedly is not to be redundant. This is detailed [in the following].

To speak of it is not to be prolix; to summarize it is not to be brief. Unifying the entire sutra into a single phrase and subsuming all affirmative statements into the negation of all phrases—this is the light of the Dharma-treasure of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, which thus illuminates both heaven and earth.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat amidst the great assembly.
He bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare it is, World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas. World-Honored One, when sons and daughters of good family resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi..."
"Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta. How should one abide? How should one subdue the mind?
This is where Subhūti pays homage, praises the Buddha, and initiates the dialogue that opens the sutra. The daily activities of the World-Honored One are the single Suchness;
he is empty of the four marks, spontaneously following conditions, and there is nothing particularly extraordinary about this. Subhūti—
Upon giving rise to a single insight, he immediately praised it as rare and marvelous. He opened a separate eye upon the crown of his head, which shared the radiance of the *ūrṇā-kośa* mark.
As his eyebrows met, he gave rise to the Buddha’s compassion of inquiry, mindfulness, and entrustment, as well as the Buddha’s teaching on abiding the mind and subduing the mind.
This was a question posed before an answer had been given. The Buddha, regarding the arousal of the Mahayana mind, bestowed [upon him...]
One who gives rise to the mind of the Supreme Vehicle is like a prince at birth, who is first bathed with the waters of the four great oceans;

this is the meaning of protective mindfulness (*anuparigraha*). When he has grown up, the family estate is entrusted to him and he is invested with the royal throne, again with the waters of the four great oceans poured upon his crown;
this is the meaning of entrustment (*parindāna*). For a bodhisattva at the initial stage, there are four aspects.

It is not yet empty; the two attachments have not been forgotten. It is like a merchant hoarding rare goods who travels through cities and states, lodging by water and traveling by mountain, finding no place at all to settle.
This is truly because the mind of restless pursuit has not ceased. Therefore, he first asks about abiding and subsequently asks about subduing.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.
Sons of good family and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should abide in this manner and subdue themselves in this manner."
"His mind was thus: 'Indeed, World-Honored One, I wish and desire to hear this.
This is the manner of responding according to the question. 'Listen attentively; I shall speak for you,' is the constant protocol for transmission and reception.
Answering according to what was asked, he said: 'Abide thus; thus subdue your mind. Only upon attaining such phrases does one come to know."
The four-line verse both originates from True Suchness (tathatā); it does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence, nor does it involve intellectual understanding.
This is why Kongsheng inclines his heart to accept it with faith, wishing and delighting to hear it. First he makes a vow, and in his mind there arises joy and gladness.
They earnestly entreated for what they desired, so that they might hear the sublime Dharma.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should abide in this manner and subdue their minds in this manner.
Regarding all categories of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation—"

Whether they have form or are formless; whether they possess perception, lack perception, or possess neither perception nor non-perception—I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to liberation.

Although in this way I liberate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, in truth there is not a single sentient being who has been liberated. Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva...
If a bodhisattva perceives the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.
This refutes the attachment of bodhisattvas who seek to deliver sentient beings.

The reason bodhisattvas are unable to abide in the mind and subdue the mind is that their concern for delivering sentient beings is so intense that they frequently give rise to deluded thoughts and make grand vows, [thinking] "sentient beings..."

The boundless vow to deliver others: to set aside oneself for the sake of others, and to contemplate placing this insignificant self among the four modes of birth and ten classes of beings, so as to universally deliver every person and perfectly accomplish the completion of every thing.

That the Buddha has "three things he cannot do," and that even Yao and Shun were still troubled by these matters—therefore, when our Buddha established his teaching, having made the boundless vow to deliver all sentient beings, he immediately withdrew [the self] back [into the source].
Regarding the statement within one's own portion, "I vow to deliver all sentient beings by their very nature":

this is because the sentient beings of the great earth are precisely the sentient beings of self-nature (*svabhāva*). A Bodhisattva who clings to appearances divides them into two, whereas a Bodhisattva of true reality (*dharmatā*) unifies them into one.
If one realizes that "I can deliver the sentient beings of self-nature," then there is self-nature nirvāṇa, lacking nothing.
There is nothing remaining. The nirvāṇa of sentient beings is also like this. This is precisely what the Confucian tradition calls "attaining the harmony of the Mean":
"Heaven and Earth find their proper places, and all things are nourished. The Sanskrit term *nirvāṇa* is translated here as "quiescent extinction" (*jīmíè*). Quiescence means immovability.
Cessation is non-arising. To be able to deliver sentient beings through quiescent cessation is to regard the six realms as one family and the eight wildernesses as a single gate.
Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things are one with me.
Immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings do not exist outside the realm of sentient beings within their own self-nature; there is not a single sentient being who is not delivered.

In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. When the Bodhisattva realizes that sentient beings are the self-nature of consciousness, his deluded thoughts are once and for all subdued.
This single phrase clarifies it: the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span are fundamentally empty.
To have nothing is to be a sage; to have something is to be an ordinary person. A Bodhisattva leads others across by means of wisdom.
This is merely a name. To abandon oneself for another, or to look toward the child while losing the mother, is not the way of a Great Bodhisattva.
Therefore, the four-line verse constitutes the essential purport of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on anything regarding phenomena.
That is to say, they should not dwell on form when practicing giving; they should not dwell on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when practicing giving.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give in this manner, not dwelling upon signs. Why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling upon signs, their merit...
The merit is inconceivable. Subhūti, what do you think? Can the space in the eastern direction be measured?
"No, World-Honored One. Subhūti, can the space in the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir be measured?
"No, World-Honored One. Subhūti, the merit of a bodhisattva’s giving without dwelling on signs is likewise thus.
"This is inconceivable, Subhūti. A bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed.
This refutes the attachment of those bodhisattvas who dwell upon signs while practicing giving in pursuit of merit.

Those who seek to create blessings and cultivate virtue harbor the four marks in their minds and remain fixed on the extreme of giving; they gradually form a habitual pattern and are unable to overturn it in an instant.
[The text] is translated as follows: One must practice giving without abiding in the four marks (*catur-nimitta*). The merit thereof is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Furthermore, "Subhūti" is a reiteration of the words of the question and answer; it addresses the one born of emptiness (*Śūnyatā-jāta*) and speaks to him.

Regarding the Dharma, a Bodhisattva should practice giving without abiding in anything. This is because the four marks are fundamentally non-existent, and the three spheres (*tri-maṇḍala*) are [empty].
Emptiness. One does not perceive a self that is able to give; one does not perceive a person to whom something is given;
one does not perceive sentient beings who practice giving; one does not perceive a recipient of merit or a long-lived being.

This applies to the eye regarding forms, the ear regarding sounds, the nose regarding odors, the tongue regarding tastes, the body regarding tangibles, and the mind regarding mental phenomena—all [are likewise empty].
He does not abide. Internally he purifies the six sense organs; externally he purifies the six sense objects.

While the sentient beings of the great earth are daily agitated within the realm of the organs, objects, and the physical world, seeking through the practice of giving, that which resides in me abides in the dharma-position, quiescent and unmoving.
It responds and thereby penetrates all; it is not necessary for everyone to practice giving, yet there is the transformative influence and the preservation of the spirit.
"Exquisite! There is not a single thing that does not find its proper place; this is what is called 'giving without dwelling upon signs.
Its merit is inconceivable. He then called out to Subhūti to further interrogate him:

"Because the world possesses signs, there are the four intermediate directions, above, and below, as well as the kalpas of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. If it were without signs, the four intermediate directions, above, and below would be void."
"Emptiness is devoid of substance; it cannot be conceived or measured. Upon these words, Haosheng attained realization.
He came to believe that the merit of practicing giving without abiding is likewise so. The Buddha then confirmed this, saying, "All Bodhisattvas should abide according to what has been taught."
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, physical marks.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever marks there are, all are empty and false. If one sees that all marks are non-marks,"
They immediately see the Tathāgata.
This is because these bodhisattvas see the Buddha through attachment to marks (*nimitta*), prostrating and seeking merit;
they do not know that beyond this sandalwood-colored form there is a true Buddha who is non-marked (*animitta*) and cannot be seen by means of attachment to marks. An ancient worthy said: "Gold..."
The Buddha is not saved by the furnace; the wooden Buddha is not saved by fire; the clay Buddha is not saved by water. The true Buddha sits within.
That which is referred to in the sutras as being "without marks" (animitta) is precisely what is meant by the true Buddha.
The various bodhisattvas grasp at the four marks and fail to recognize markless true emptiness. Therefore, the Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever has marks..."

The self, persons, sentient beings, and so forth, are all false and illusory. Even if one diligently engages in silent contemplation, as long as subject and object have not been forgotten, it remains an illusory view.
Only when one perceives that all marks are non-marks can one be said to have personally seen the Tathāgata.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases, will give rise to true faith?

The Buddha told Subhūti: "Do not speak thus. After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, who will be able to give rise to faith in these words and phrases and regard them as true. When this was said, Subhūti...
Subhūti, you should know that such persons have not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;

rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable thousands of myriads of Buddhas. Subhūti, when they hear these phrases and give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment, the Tathāgata knows them all and sees them all. These sentient beings shall obtain such immeasurable merit.
“Virtue. Why is this? These sentient beings no longer possess the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life-span.

They have no mark of dharmas, nor do they have any mark of non-dharmas. Why is this? If these sentient beings take up marks with their minds, they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.
If they take up the mark of dharmas, they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a being, and a life-span.”
Why is this? If one grasps at the marks of what is not the Dharma, one is immediately attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.
Therefore, one should not grasp at the Dharma, nor should one grasp at what is not the Dharma. For this reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that my teaching of the Dharma is like the parable of a raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."

This repeated dialogue explains that, beyond the four marks, the Bodhisattva separately gives rise to attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), grasping at the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and non-phenomena (*adharmalakṣaṇa*);
thus, they have ultimately not yet realized true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As the Tathāgata himself once said:
"In the forty-nine years I have remained in the world, I have never spoken a single word. A sutra states: "Know that my preaching of the Dharma is like..."

Regarding the parable of the raft: it is because bodhisattvas at the initial stage have not yet forgotten their attachment to dharmas that, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases, they immediately give rise to genuine faith.
Starting from the observance of precepts and the cultivation of merit, they believe and uphold them with earnest conviction.

The roots of goodness they plant are firmly due to what was planted in previous lives; yet, although they possess genuine faith, it is not yet ultimate. They must wait to hear these chapters and verses [to reach completion].
Even for one who, until not a single thought arises, gives rise to pure faith, their merit is immeasurable. What is called "substantial faith" involves grasping at signs;

it consists of observing precepts and cultivating blessings, which plant the causes of outflows. Even if one possesses roots of goodness spanning many kalpas, [it remains within the realm of conditioned existence].
Cultivating and planting roots of merit from the presence of one Buddha up to ten million Buddhas results in the karmic rewards of humans and devas;
yet what is ultimately attained remains finite and limited. This is not as excellent as a single moment of pure faith. In a single thought-moment, the four marks of existence are entirely empty;
in pure faith, the six sense objects do not abide. There is not a single dharma that can be grasped. This is...

This is called "truly attaining. In the past, when Master Fu ascended the seat to lecture on the sutras, he struck the lectern with his ruler once and immediately declared, "The lecture on the sutras is finished.
This is a model of single-minded pure faith. Possessing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and attaining the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, the path of resonance and response is joined;
both speaker and listener possess immeasurable merit and virtue that is inconceivable.

Furthermore, as for the passage beginning with "Why is this so? it serves to clarify the meaning of the four-line verse. If one can empty oneself of the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), then both dharma and non-dharma will dissolve and return to non-existence.
Conversely, to be attached to marks or to grasp at marks constitutes attachment to dharmas (*dharma-abhiniveśa*); thus, one must certainly not grasp at or be attached to either dharma or non-dharma.
Moreover, there is concern that bodhisattvas who harbor attachment to dharmas might [misunderstand] the upholding of the sutra...

The Director followed the instructions and practiced accordingly, just as the Buddha had taught. Yet he did not recognize the Buddha’s mind, nor did he realize that the Dharma spoken by the Buddha is called the "Prajñā-boat.
As long as one has not yet crossed the ford of delusion, one must rely on boats and rafts; once one has reached the other shore, what further use is there for a vessel?

The Sixth Patriarch said: "When deluded, the teacher ferries you across; when awakened, you ferry yourself across. It is like forgetting the trap once the fish is caught, or [forgetting] the snare once the rabbit is caught.

Forgetting the tracks [of the hoof]. One who has attained mastery of the essential Dharma should be like this. Only after recognizing the four-line verse may one recite the sutras and peruse the Tripitaka.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

“Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? “Subhūti, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has preached, there is no fixed dharma called ‘anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,’ nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach.”
Why is this? All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas. Why is this so?
Because all worthy ones and sages are distinguished from one another precisely by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Continuing from the preceding text, this section restates the meaning of the aforementioned attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

Fearing that bodhisattvas at the initial stage might stubbornly cling to the Buddha’s words as being ultimate—thinking, "The Buddha has already attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment"—and thus grasp them as fixed, definitive phenomena, thereby forming an attachment to dharmas, [the Buddha] does not wait for Subhūti’s question but first interrogates him. Will Subhūti indeed be able to understand?
The Buddha has taught that there is no fixed dharma called "unsurpassed enlightenment," nor is there any fixed dharma that can be spoken.
Why is this? All teachings spoken by the Tathāgata flow forth from the light of prajñā;
those who listen cannot grasp them, and those who speak cannot transmit them. If sentient beings take up signs with their minds, they immediately become attached.
Regarding the four marks: grasping at the mark of phenomena (*dharma*) and the mark of non-phenomena (*adharma*), one is attached to all four marks.

Since both "this is dharma" and "this is adharma" are ultimately non-dharmas, one has not yet realized the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and of phenomena. Both belong to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); one must empty these two attachments.
This is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The dharma of the unconditioned is the school of formlessness (*animitta*). It is like water being poured from one vessel to another:
those who receive it shallowly become worthy persons (*satpuruṣa*), while those who receive it deeply become sages (*ārya*). Although there are distinctions, in reality there are no distinctions.
As for the four fruits of sagehood and worthiness discussed in the subsequent chapter, all their differences arise from within the dharma of the unconditioned.
Only when one reaches the ultimate fruit of the Tathāgata and the four marks are entirely empty can it be said that, regarding the Dharma, there is truly nothing to be attained.

Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One."
Why is this? This merit is not, in its true nature, merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if there were someone who, from this sutra, were to receive, uphold, and even explain as little as a single four-line verse to others, their merit would surpass the former.
Why is this? Subhūti, it is because all Buddhas and the unsurpassed... [of all Buddhas]... arise from this Dharma.]
The Dharma of *samyaksambodhi* all issues from this sutra. Subhūti, that which is called the Buddha-dharma is, in fact, not the Buddha-dharma.
Continuing from the preceding text, this further dispels the attachment to performing acts of giving based on signs (*nimitta*).

This refers to practicing giving while dwelling within the six sense organs and six sense objects, discriminating between the signs of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. Such is called a matter pertaining to the extreme of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Because many bodhisattvas, following the common inclination to seek merit, give rise to views and practice generosity by exhausting their wealth and strength with all seven treasures,
filling an extent equal to a trichiliocosm and extending throughout the sentient beings of that trichiliocosm—
the merit they thereby obtain should be equivalent [to that of Śūnyatā], without waiting for it to be produced by emptiness.

Question: Previously, [the Buddha] interrogated him. Śūnyatā-utpāda was indeed able to believe with clarity that within the portion of merit, there is both phenomenon (*dharma*) and nature (*dharmatā*).
The gift of the seven treasures is the phenomenon of merit; because phenomena have degrees of magnitude, the Tathāgata said that the merit is great.
The four-line verse from the sutra, which one expounds for others, is the nature of merit; this nature neither increases nor decreases.
He bestowed the Dharma upon others, who heard and accepted it, attaining realization at the mere mention of his words. This is the ability to exhaust one's own nature and the nature of others;
the merit therein cannot be matched by the seven treasures of a great trichiliocosm, and is therefore said to surpass them.
In the past, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he pointed directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature one becomes a Buddha. His [teaching] before the Emperor...

He said: "To serve the Buddha is fundamentally without merit; it is not that merit is fundamentally non-existent, but rather that within the original nature there is no mark of merit. Furthermore, he addressed Subhūti to clarify this, saying:
"The reason why a four-line verse from the Sūtra surpasses the value of the seven treasures is because it contains the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened, wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas."
This emerges from this sutra. To explain it for others is why the gift of Dharma (dharmadāna) is far superior to the gift of material wealth (āmiṣadāna).
Previously, the attachment to abiding in signs was refuted by means of signlessness (animitta); here, the attachment to the gift of material wealth is refuted by means of the gift of Dharma.
The underlying intent is different. Furthermore, fearing that bodhisattvas might mistake the gift of Dharma for a uniquely superior merit, he speaks again.
Śūnyatā-janman said: "That which is called the Buddha-dharma is not the true Buddha-dharma; it is merely the Buddha-dharma of the four-line verses found within the sutras.
To truly know where the Buddha-dharma resides: my teaching has come from the West, and it does not establish written words.
Written words are the dharma of sentient beings. Only when one realizes that every phenomenon is fundamentally without dharma, and that there is neither dharma nor non-dharma, is it so."
This is the true Buddha-dharma.
Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) have the thought, "I have attained the fruit of stream-entry"?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A stream-enterer is called one who has 'entered the stream,' yet..."
There is no entering. One does not enter into form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena;
this is called a *srotāpanna*. Subhūti, what do you think? Does a *sakṛdāgāmin* have the thought, "I have attained the fruit of a *sakṛdāgāmin*"?
Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A *sakṛdāgāmin* is so named because they return once more, yet in reality there is no coming or going."
This is called a Sakṛdāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have this thought:
"I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin"? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that?
An Anāgāmin is called 'one who does not come back,' yet in reality there is no such thing as 'not coming back. For this reason, he is called an Anāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think?
"How is it? Can an Arhat have this thought: 'I have attained the path of Arhatship'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because there is truly no dharma that is called 'Arhat.
World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have this thought, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' he would thereby be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span."
“World-Honored One, the Buddha has declared that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention and am foremost among men;
I am a foremost arhat free from desire. World-Honored One, I do not harbor the thought: ‘I am an arhat free from desire.
World-Honored One, if I were to harbor such a thought as ‘I have attained the path of arhatship,’ then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti delights in emptiness.”
"Āraṇāvihārin, because Subhūti actually has no practice, he is called 'Subhūti who delights in the practice of araṇā.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: 'What do you think? When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, did he obtain any dharma?
'No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, regarding the dharma...'"
"In truth, nothing is attained.

This承接 (continues from) the preceding text. Regarding what was said—that all noble sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)—the answers given according to the capacities of the questioners lead them gradually into deeper understanding.
This explains the basis for the differentiation of the first, second, third, and fourth fruits of the path (*phala*).

To distinguish their characteristics and explain them in sequence: the *srotāpanna* is called "one who has entered the stream. This means that having first entered its gate, they have attained inclusion within the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*).
They are able to abandon coarse and heavy afflictions (*kleśa*), yet are not yet able to be free from subtle afflictions;

this is called the first fruit (*phala*). The *sakṛdāgāmin* is called "one who comes back once. This is because, through self-observation of various objects, they [have reached the point where] there is only...
One birth and one extinction; there is no second birth or extinction. In reality, no birth or extinction can be apprehended. This is called the second fruit.
As for the *anāgāmin*, it is named "one who does not return," meaning they do not return to take birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The mind has nothing to be attained, and in reality, there is no characteristic of non-returning. This is called the third fruit. As for the *arhat*, this is translated as...

"Those beyond training" refers to those whose outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted; there is no further need for cultivation. Although dharmas exist, in reality there is not a single dharma to be apprehended.
This is called the fourth fruit. Subhūti is such a noble one who has attained the fourth fruit; he now presents his own realization.
Therefore it is said: "An Arhat does not cling to the four marks and does not form the thought, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship.
He recalls that he received the Buddha’s prediction, saying: 'I have attained the Samādhi of Non-contention; I am foremost among men.'"

He is called an Arhat free from desire. If, at the time of receiving the prediction, I had directly accepted it, saying of myself, "I am an Arhat free from desire," then there would have been a real dharma being practiced by me;
the World-Honored One certainly would not have granted me the prediction as one who practices the path of tranquility. For the noble ones of the four fruits abide in unconditioned dharmas.
Yet there is a distinction such as this. This [attainment] still pertains to the stage of an Arhat; when one reaches the ultimate fruit of a Tathāgata, that is the absolute limit.
One should know that on that day, the World-Honored One personally received the prediction of enlightenment from Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Tasting the unconditioned dharmas, there is truly nothing to be attained. Although one speaks of receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), it merely seals this very mind;

it does not mean that there is a dharma to be obtained or a Buddha to be realized. This refutes the various Bodhisattvas' attachment to seeking the realization of fruits and receiving predictions for the attainment of Buddhahood.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is that?
That which is called 'adorning a buddha-field' is not actually adorning; it is merely designated as 'adornment.
Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should give rise to a pure mind in this way: they should not give rise to a mind by dwelling on form."
"When one dwells upon sounds, smells, tastes, touches, or dharmas to give rise to the mind, one should give rise to that mind without dwelling on anything.
This refutes the attachment to adorning Buddha-lands through the mark of dwelling. This principle encompasses both the coarse and the subtle.
At the subtle level, it refers to the adornment of the myriad virtues within the Buddha-nature of one's own mind; it cannot be sought through marks, nor can it be beheld with the eyes.
The Way is adornment; yet it is not adornment. That which is thus called adornment is the adornment that exists inherently within one’s own nature.
Coarse forms include building temples, constructing stupas, molding images, and copying scriptures—all such conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
The Way is adornment; yet it is not adornment. One must forget both subject and object; only then is it called adornment.

This is solemnity. When the Tathāgata posed his inquiry, Subhūti attained realization and understanding. One should know that the adornment of a Buddha-land is the pure mind, the mind free from abiding characteristics.

Should there be even a single instance of a mind that clings to abiding, it will be bound by external objects and unable to be agile and autonomous—much like withered wood that no longer sprouts or dead ashes that no longer burn. Yet such a person would still claim it to be "adornment."
This is not true adornment. One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere.

This is the adamantine true eye, the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*, the direct pointing and single transmission—the most intimate and vital phrase. In the past, the Sixth Patriarch heard it once while atop his firewood pole and was immediately enlightened;
he entered the chamber of Huangmei and directly took responsibility for it. All who belong to the lineage of the Patriarchs [must do likewise].
One must seek a point of resolution from the place where the mind arises from non-abiding. It must not be treated as mere words or texts, nor accepted in a state of blind ignorance.
Only when it accords with the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West is it truly the adornment of the Buddha-land.
Examining the ancient composition of characters: the arising of the mind constitutes nature (*xing*). Nature is like flowing water; if it does not arise, it dries up.
Nature is like a forest of trees; if it does not arise, it withers and breaks. Nature is like a living fire; if it does not arise, it is extinguished.
Nature is like the lunar disc; if it does not arise, it wanes. The movement of heaven and earth never ceases day or night; the mechanism of the myriad things revolves without rest. Thus it is said:
Because there is no abiding, there is no non-arising. Its self-nature is suchness; fundamentally there is no dwelling or attachment, and fundamentally there is no arising or ceasing.
To recognize this mind that arises without abiding is precisely the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Subhūti, it is as if there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think? Would that body be large?
Subhūti replied, "It would be very large, World-Honored One. Why is this? The Buddha has taught that what is not a body is called a 'great body'."
Continuing from the preceding discussion on the adornment of Buddha-lands, this is a response given according to the capacity of the questioner.

One realizes that the adornment of the Buddha-land does not cling to substantial characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and does not fall into the categories of "small" or "great. Suppose there were someone who, practicing contemplation based on characteristics, enters the provisional through emptiness;
if the sixteen-foot golden body suddenly becomes as vast as Mount Sumeru, this remains merely a matter of attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). Why is this so?
Therefore, the pure *dharmakāya* has neither smallness nor greatness. The Buddha taught that what is not a body is the true *dharmakāya*;
thus it is called the "great body.
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—what do you think?
"What do you think? Are all those Ganges rivers many? Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One.
Even the Ganges rivers alone are already countless, let alone their sands. "Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth:
if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the seven treasures, filled as many great trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges rivers..."
"If one were to give as a gift a thousand worlds, would the merit obtained be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One.

The Buddha told Subhūti, "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, should even receive and uphold a four-line verse or the like and explain it for others, this merit would surpass the former merit."
These three [points] refute the attachment to the notion that giving for the sake of seeking merit is superior;
for all Bodhisattvas give with the seven treasures, and that which is more is considered superior. The Buddha addressed Subhūti with a question, saying, "The Ganges is the most numerous;
are the sands within it beyond the reach of calculation and reckoning? Is this not many? Subhūti followed the question.
He replied immediately, without allowing for any deliberation. The Buddha used the metaphor of jewels and sand;

if one were to fill the entire world-system with such jewels and offer them as alms, the vastness of the merit obtained would be beyond description. He then told him that it was better to receive and uphold even a single four-line verse from within this sutra.
Regarding those who explain it for others: this is the gift of Dharma, whereas that [other person] is the gift of material wealth;
its merit is so preeminent that it cannot be matched by the seven treasures filling the Ganges. "Receiving" means to accept with sincere faith.

"Upholding" means to maintain and practice it; it is not merely like superficial recitation. For one who explains it to others, the four marks are entirely empty, and thus it is not something to be explained.
Thus it is said: "When both person and dharma are forgotten, one speaks without speaking. I speak by means of non-speaking;
others hear by means of non-hearing. This is called true exposition and true merit."

Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even as little as a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by the entire world—including its devas, humans, and asuras—as if it were a stupa or temple of the Buddha.
How much more so for one who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it in its entirety? Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme and foremost rarity.
Regarding the existence of this Dharma: wherever this sutra is located, there is a Buddha, as well as his honored disciples.

Continuing from the preceding text, he addressed Subhūti, saying: "Upon hearing this sutra being preached, even down to a single four-line stanza, one should conceive the thought that it is rare and difficult to encounter.
It is not only the assembly of bodhisattvas who should respectfully receive and uphold it; so too should the world."
Devas and humans, even asuras and others, shall all pay respectful homage and make offerings [to this] as if it were the Buddha himself, a stūpa, or a temple.
The radiance of the Dharma-treasure illuminates heaven and earth; it is inconceivable.
How much more so for a blind person who upholds this sutra, whose practice and understanding correspond, who recites this sutra with mind and mouth in perfect accord—such a one...
A person, being able to remain without leaving their original place, can accomplish the most rare and marvelous Dharma.
This Dharma shall circulate through every phenomenon without interruption. Wherever the scriptures are found, there is the Buddha.
Upon the assembly of the Vajra, the honored disciples—such as Subhūti and others—will fill the void of space, neither being anywhere nor not being anywhere.
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named?
How should we uphold it? The Buddha told Subhūti, "This sutra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
By this name, you should uphold it. Why is this so? Subhūti, when the Buddha speaks of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it is precisely..."
"It is not the perfection of wisdom; it is called the perfection of wisdom. "Subhūti, what do you think?
Has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has preached nothing."
Before the Dharma assembly had concluded, he suddenly requested the title of the sutra. This was because upon reaching this point, Subhūti had already attained wondrous realization;

with that single question posed in the midst of the discourse, he cut off all currents of conceptualization and opened a separate path. To further clarify the preceding text, the compiler has provided this additional explanation.

Students should know that from this point on, one enters deeply into the gate of the magnificent mansion; it must not be considered sufficient to achieve only a small measure of understanding. Respectfully submitted.
The meaning of "holding" and "understanding" is as explained above. Regarding the phrase "the Buddha spoke the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*," and so forth:

it means that this Dharma was directly issued from the Buddha’s own mouth; therefore, it is called "spoken by the Buddha. It silently transmits the Buddha’s mind and transcends what can be expressed in words.

Although there is something attained, in reality there is nothing to be attained; therefore, it is said to be "not. That which is "not" is precisely that which "is. One forcibly bestows a name upon it.
Therefore, it says, "This is called. There is no room for further addition in the explanation of the sutra title.

After the name of the sutra has been set forth and the World-Honored One has finished preaching the Dharma, he fears that the assembly of Bodhisattvas, having simultaneously heard and received it, might grasp only its superficial meaning and all conclude that the Tathāgata has actually preached some dharma.
Thus, he calls out to Subhūti to interrogate him. Subhūti was indeed able to [respond] secretly...
Contemplating its intent: one must directly accept it as it is. A single phrase reveals it all: "The Tathāgata has, in truth, nothing to teach.
How direct and straightforward this is! As for the Dharma that is taught and the person who teaches it—the Tathāgata is empty of both person and dharma;
subject and object are both extinguished. How could there be any further appearance of teaching the Dharma? Only upon reaching this point does one truly know the Yellow... [text ends].
Facing the Old Master, his compassionate heart is overflowing.
Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms contained within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system many?
Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One. Subhūti, those atoms which the Tathāgata has spoken of are, in truth, not atoms.
Dust. This is called "minute dust. The Tathāgata says that the world is not a world; this is called "the world. This follows from the preceding text:
the Dharma that is preached is not a dull emptiness. It is because the realms of dust have been melted away and fused into a single essence;
right and wrong have been pulverized and subsumed into true emptiness. The lush green bamboo is entirely True Suchness (Tathatā). Lush...
The deep yellow flowers are none other than Prajñā. Manifesting the great as small, a single atom is a world-system; manifesting the small as great, a world-system is a single atom.
The entire body of the Vajra is nowhere that is not the Dharmakāya; the true light of Prajñā, wherever it may be, becomes the Dharma-treasure.
This is that which cannot be spoken, yet there is nothing that is not the Dharma that is spoken. Thus, the Buddha, at [the place marked by □]...
They sat. One question and one answer; like a needle meeting its eye, they were perfectly matched. Only those who awaken can know when the notes of the musical scale fall into exquisite harmony.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? "No, World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that the thirty-two..."
The two marks are themselves no-marks; this is called the thirty-two marks.
This follows from the preceding passage on the melting away of the realms of dust and worlds; therefore, the Dharma-transformation is as one.

The true reality (*dharmatā*) of the three bodies—Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya—is neither existent nor non-existent. Nevertheless, when the assembly of Bodhisattvas gazes up at the compassionate countenance, they all [perceive it] through the thirty-two [marks].
One gives rise to views based on appearances, yet fails to realize that these are merely the Tathāgata of form-and-appearance (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
One should know that there is another, the True Nature Tathāgata (*tathatā-tathāgata*), which is neither form nor emptiness, transcending all myriad phenomena, immutable and indestructible.
It dissolves back into the midst of the four marks; therefore it is said: "These marks are themselves non-marks. To recognize this non-mark is called the Real.
This is the mark, Subhūti.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who give away their lives as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River,
and yet another person, from within this sutra, were to even receive and uphold a single four-line verse or the like and explain it to others— [the latter would generate more merit].
The merit thereof is exceedingly great.

This is called the "retribution of merit. It dispels the attachment to giving while clinging to signs (*nimitta*). The previous mention of giving the seven treasures refers to relinquishing external objects and seeking outwardly;
this present mention of giving one's body and life refers to realizing that the illusory body is a fabrication of illusion.
Although one may relinquish this illusory body, it is ultimately not the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). One must believe, accept, and uphold these four-line verses;
awaken to the fact that the four marks—the self, person, sentient being, and life-span—are entirely non-existent; realize that the three spheres are empty in essence; and explain them for others.
When both person and dharma are forgotten, benefiting both self and others, this is the ultimate. That its merit is "very great" refers to the *prajñā* [of these verses].
This merit pervades all sentient beings; it is inconceivable.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent. With tears streaming down his face and weeping with grief, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare it is, World-Honored One! That the Buddha should preach such a profound sutra as this. From the past until now, the wisdom I have attained..."

“O World-Honored One, we have never before heard such a sutra as this. World-Honored One, if there should be anyone who hears this sutra and their mind of faith becomes pure, they will immediately give rise to the mark of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). You should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
World-Honored One, this mark of reality is precisely the absence of marks; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name ‘mark of reality.’”
The preceding passage stated that his merit would be exceedingly great; here it is called the "supremely rare merit. Compared to the merit previously obtained, this is indeed truly rare.
When Subhūti heard this sutra, he realized and entered the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*).
This was not comparable to his prior karmic reward. His joy reached its peak, yet he wept out of sorrow, rejoicing in the profundity of the Dharma he had heard. Furthermore—
Lamenting his late encounter [with the Dharma], Subhūti spoke to the Buddha without waiting for further questioning; this was his presentation of understanding after his realization.
Although Subhūti had already attained the eye of wisdom and perceived the truth within existence, because he had not yet heard this sutra, he still possessed a residual obstruction of emptiness.
Having heard this sutra, he was further led beyond even emptiness; he thoroughly realized the Middle Way and clearly perceived the true reality (*dharmatā*).
He addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "If there should be another person who hears what I have heard, they too shall attain what I have attained.
The merits within the sutra will arrive spontaneously without being sought. Thus, amidst the myriad phenomena and the dense array of all signs—which are all illusory—he pointed out the reality.
The *xiàng* (mark/sign) is the root of all meritorious virtues; it is the self-nature (*svabhāva*). If self-nature were non-existent, meritorious virtues would likewise be non-existent.
Once one realizes self-nature, meritorious virtues are found to be inherently present.

What is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely the purity of the mind of faith, the wondrous and profound *dhāraṇī*, eternally empty and eternally quiescent. The entire great treasury of the teachings is subsumed within this portion of self-nature.
There is no Dharma that can be spoken; there is no Buddha to be realized; there is no birth from which to deliver beings.

This is called the accomplishment of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), the foremost rare merit. What is said in the sutras regarding "merit" (*puṇya*) and "virtue" (*guṇa*) taken together is spoken for the sake of those with middling faculties.
To speak here solely of "merit" (*guṇa*) indicates the moment when the fruit of this merit has been perfected; the retribution of worldly fortune (*puṇyavipāka*) is not worth mentioning.
The *Platform Sūtra* states that virtue resides within the Dharma-body and does not reside in the realm of worldly blessings; this is precisely what is meant here.

Fearing that the Bodhisattvas, upon hearing the teaching of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), might take it to be a substantial reality and seek it by clinging to signs—thereby straying far from the Way—Subhūti addressed the Buddha once more, saying: "That which is called the true mark is like the great void; it is without marks."
It can be sought; therefore, it is said that this is precisely the absence of marks (*animitta*).

Furthermore, fearing that upon hearing the teaching of the absence of marks, one might abandon the reality and grasp at emptiness, mistaking it for the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit, and fail to realize that the original true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely the absence of marks—neither existent nor non-existent, neither empty nor real—it is just like the taste of salt in water or the lacquer-blue within color: it definitely exists, yet...
Because one perceives its form, the Tathāgata calls it the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
World-Honored One, for me now to hear such a sūtra and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it is not difficult.
However, if in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this sūtra, can believe, understand, accept, and uphold it—such persons [are truly rare].

This is truly the most rare and marvelous thing. Why is this? Because such a person has no mark of self, no mark of others, no mark of sentient beings, and no mark of a life-span. And why? Because the mark of self is precisely no-mark;
the marks of others, sentient beings, and a life-span are likewise no-marks. Why is this? Because one who is free from all marks is called a Buddha. Buddha.
He addressed Subhūti: "So it is, so it is. If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is most rare."
Following the previous section on the first rare merit, this passage speaks only of "rare"; thus, the merit would be insufficient to discuss.
After Subhūti had attained realization, he preached the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them all to return to that same realization.

He first states that his own hearing of this sutra, along with his faith, understanding, acceptance, and upholding of it, is not yet to be considered difficult; rather, he wishes [to speak of] those of the future.

Five hundred years constitute one small kalpa. That all sentient beings should possess the same faith and understanding, and the same practice and upholding, is a rare and difficult-to-attain condition. Why is this?

Because those who recognize even a single four-line verse within this sutra are able to empty themselves of the four marks: the self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span. This is the Way.
This is signlessness (*animitta*). It is precisely the absence of signs. This sign and the absence of signs—both views are abandoned.

Being equal to the Buddha, it is said that "this very name is the Buddha. That the Buddha then confirmed, "So it is, so it is," means that [Subhūti] profoundly accords with the essential Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Subhūti further feared that sentient beings of future generations might treat the Mahāyāna sūtras as something vast and distant like a great river.

It is said: "Gazing out at the vast ocean, one retreats. To truly receive, believe, and uphold [this teaching] is difficult to find anyone who can do so. This is truly because the mental capacity of sentient beings is narrow and inferior;
they see little and are easily startled by much, being alarmed upon encountering the great and terrified upon meeting the lofty. They feel dread when facing what is difficult.
Only those who can carefully enter through hearing into faith, and who, by means of that faith, dispel doubt, remaining calm and unalarmed, serene and undaunted, and resolute, are capable of this.
To fearlessly believe, accept, and uphold [this teaching] is truly the foremost and most rare merit.
One should know that such a person is exceedingly rare; their merit is beyond comparison.
Why is this? Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the "first pāramitā" is not actually the first pāramitā;
it is designated as the "first pāramitā."
This follows the preceding text and offers a further interpretation.

In the preceding section, Subhūti, having heard the sutra and attained awakening, further made a great vow to circulate these verses of the sutra throughout the Dharma-realm, reaching all sentient beings even five hundred years hence, so that each person may hear the sutra, each may believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, thereby emptying themselves of the four marks and remaining without alarm, without fear, and without dread. This...
This empty space gives rise to a single fragment of compassionate heart, a gift of Dharma that is the ultimate principle. The World-Honored One called out to him and said:
"The gift of Dharma you have bestowed is the foremost and final realization. You should know that all sentient beings possess this one true scripture;
it is secretly stored within the Tathāgatagarbha. To awaken to it is to be a Buddha; to be deluded by it is to be a sentient being."
Ultimately, there is no Buddha to be attained; there is nothing born to be saved; there is no dharma to be bestowed; and there is no shore to be reached.
When the Buddha speaks of giving as the foremost *pāramitā*, it is not actually the foremost *pāramitā*;

it is merely a provisional name used to enable people to recognize and grasp the "other shore. It is simply a designation for that which one first ascends and reaches directly. Regarding the *pāramitās*: [text continues].
Ten: first, giving; second, ethical discipline; third, patience; fourth, diligence; fifth, meditative concentration;
sixth, wisdom; seventh, loving-kindness; eighth, compassion; ninth, skillful means; tenth, non-retrogression. Here, the term "first" refers specifically to giving.
The former was taught for the sake of seeking merit; this is taught for the sake of liberating sentient beings.
Subhūti, the perfection of patience spoken of by the Tathāgata is not a perfection of patience; it is called the "perfection of patience."

Continuing from the preceding text: regarding the giving of one’s body and life, there is yet another interpretation. The former belongs to the category of *dāna* (giving), while this belongs to *kṣānti* (patience).

This is because practicing giving by relinquishing the body and ending one's life represents the ultimate limit of *dāna*, whereas being without anger, resentment, vexation, or affliction represents the ultimate limit of *kṣānti*. This is that which enables one to reach the further shore (*pāramitā*) in its finality.

O person, you should know that there is yet another step beyond this. When the four marks do not exist and the three wheels are empty in essence—where there is no giver, no recipient of the gift, and no insult to be endured, and no shore to be reached—this alone is the ultimate of ultimates.
Therefore, the Buddha said to Subhūti: "The Tathāgata speaks of patience, yet it is not patience; it is merely a provisional designation."
He said: "It is merely for others to take it upon themselves.

Why is this? Subhūti, when in the past I was dismembered by King Kali, at that time I had no perception of a self, no perception of a person, no perception of a sentient being, and no perception of a life-span. Why is this? Because at that time I..."
