In the past, when my limbs were being severed joint by joint, if there had been any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.
Subhūti, furthermore, I recall that during five hundred lifetimes I was a rishi of patience;
throughout those lifetimes, there was no notion of a self, no notion of a person, no notion of a sentient being, and no notion of a life-span.

Continuing from the preceding discussion on patience (*kṣānti*): the World-Honored One manifested his body and preached the Dharma, extracting the paradigm of patience from within his own sphere of realization;
only upon reaching this point does one arrive at the ultimate limit. Formerly, five hundred lifetimes ago, the World-Honored One was a *rṣi* (sage) named Kṣāntivādin.
While he sat in meditative seclusion in the mountains, he encountered King Kali, who had gone out hunting. The king paused there for a brief rest. To his left...
The aforementioned court lady went to see the rishi and circumambulated him in worship. When the king became aware of this, he grew furious and mutilated the rishi’s limbs.
The rishi received it with joy and made a vow, saying: "May I, in birth after birth throughout all ages, deliver the king so that he may attain Buddhahood.
This was indeed the giving of one's own body and life; even as his limbs were being severed joint by joint, he felt no [aversion].

Regarding anger and resentment: there is nothing particularly extraordinary about them other than the fact that all things are empty. There is no self that undergoes cutting or dismemberment; there is no person who performs the cutting or dismembering;
there are no sentient beings subject to karmic retribution; and there is no life-principle that clings to the body out of delusion.

Furthermore, one must resolve grievances and untie karmic knots, only ceasing once they have been delivered to Buddhahood; this is what it means to practice giving while possessing the capacity for patience.
The passage beginning with "Reflecting on the past" is a retrospective account of prior causes, serving as a model for future practitioners of giving.
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should set out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by relinquishing all marks.
One should not give rise to the mind dwelling on forms; one should not give rise to the mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas.
One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere. If the mind dwells anywhere, it is not dwelling at all. Therefore, the Buddha has said that the mind of a bodhisattva is...
One should not abide in form when practicing giving. Subhūti, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, a bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner.
The Tathāgata has said that all marks are indeed no-marks; he has also said that all sentient beings are indeed no-sentient-beings.

Continuing from the preceding text: regarding generosity and forbearance spoken of in terms of being free from all marks (*animitta*), [the Buddha] tells Subhūti that the Tathāgata delivers sentient beings while remaining free from marks, and that all bodhisattvas likewise ought to resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta while remaining free from all marks.
What is meant by "being free from marks" does not refer to empty vacuity; rather, it refers to [remaining detached] amidst the turbulence of the six sense objects. All...
In the convergence of all phenomena, the myriad forms of the universe are arrayed, yet the single truth alone is revealed. One should not dwell in attachment to what is seen or heard;

it is likewise with odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharmas*). What was previously stated—that "one should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere"—indicates the fusion of object and mind.
What is now stated—that "one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere"—indicates the transformation of the mind according to the object. If...
If the mind has a place where it dwells, it is neither integrated nor transformed. To intentionally arrange one’s thoughts is itself non-dwelling.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that the Bodhisattva’s true mind for saving sentient beings should not dwell on the periphery of the six sense objects while practicing giving.
Giving with attachment to signs yields limited benefit; giving while detached from signs yields infinite benefit. Thus...

It says, "One should practice giving in this manner. Furthermore, fearing that the Bodhisattva might follow sentient beings in clinging to signs—identifying signs as the self and sentient beings as persons, thereby dividing signs and sentient beings into two—the Buddha, as soon as they were established, swept them away.
To speak of these marks is to say they are no-marks. To speak of sentient beings is to say they are no-sentient-beings. Sentient beings are the marks;
the marks are sentient beings.
Subhūti, the Tathāgata speaks what is true, speaks what is real, speaks according to reality, speaks without deception, and does not...
Regarding "different words": Subhūti, as for the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata, this Dharma is neither real nor unreal.
Following the previous passage where the title of the sutra was set forth, the Buddha preached the Dharma for Subhūti (Ākāśagambhīra).

Having delved deeper into the teaching until he spoke of how both cause and effect are empty, he feared that the listener might give rise to doubt, thinking that since the fruit is empty, there is no need for the cause.

Because of emptiness, one cannot obtain a result. Furthermore, when practicing giving within the causal stage, if one does not dwell upon the arising of a [grasping] mind, then there is no substantial fruit to be realized.
Without waiting for a question, the World-Honored One cautioned him not to doubt, but rather to believe with clarity.
The Buddha’s words are true speech without falsehood, real speech without delusion, speech as it is without change, non-deceptive speech without guile, and speech that is not otherwise.
There is no distinction between words. The Dharma heard by Śūnyatā-janman is precisely the Dharma attained by the Tathāgata.
Whether one speaks of it as real or as empty, both are but conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*); one must not rashly give rise to doubt.
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva dwells with a mind fixed on phenomena while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing at all.

If a bodhisattva practices giving with a mind that does not dwell on phenomena, it is like a person with eyes, when the light of the sun shines upon them, seeing all manner of forms. Subhūti, in future ages, if there are good men or good women...
Whoever can receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra is known by the Tathāgata through the Buddha’s wisdom;
such a person is seen by the Tathāgata, and all shall attain the accomplishment of immeasurable and boundless merit.

These words of Subhūti reiterate the profound intent of the Dharma-giving. When one transforms and delivers sentient beings with the mind of a bodhisattva, if the mind dwells upon dharmas while practicing giving, one immediately forms an attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), thereby giving rise to a hindrance to dharmas.
This is like entering a dark room where nothing at all can be seen. However, if one can practice giving without dwelling upon dharmas, [the mind] opens wide.

The Dharma-eye beholds the light of the Dharma; like a person with sight who sees the ground clearly, yet further relies upon the sunlight so that all various forms and appearances are illuminated without exception, he then called upon Ākāśagarbha and entrusted him with it, saying: "Receive and uphold this sutra."
It shall be transmitted to the future, so that all people may receive, uphold, read, and recite it. The wisdom of such a person shall enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
the illumination of the Tathāgata’s wisdom shall likewise be so. Through the mutual resonance of cause and effect, they shall know all and see all.
They accomplish immeasurable merit that is inconceivable; this is the wondrous function of practicing giving while abiding in the mark of non-abiding.
Subhūti, if there are good men or good women who, during the first part of the day, [offer] bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River...

During the middle part of the day, he again gives away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; during the latter part of the day, he likewise gives away bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
In this manner, he gives away his body for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

Yet if there were another person who, upon hearing this sutra, believes it with a mind free from opposition, their merit would surpass that of the former; how much more so if they copy it or receive it [in faith]?
To uphold, recite, and explain it for others.
This follows from the preceding discussion on giving without dwelling on signs (*animitta*). The former was shallow and the latter is profound.

What was previously taught in the sūtra did not specify the time periods or the measure of equal portions; this [passage] speaks of three times a day and of quantities equal to the sands of the Ganges River.
Regarding the phrase "the physical body does not equal the life-root": this does not refer to the previous explanation of giving away one's body and life.
Rather, it refers to manifesting various bodies at all times and in all places to practice giving throughout successive kalpas.

While the preceding sutra merely speaks of receiving and upholding [the teaching], this speaks of having faith and not being contrary to it; this is to be in accord with Prajñā until reaching the stage of non-doubt.
One should follow with a single mind and practice according to the teachings; it is not merely a matter of receiving and upholding them.
To transcribe, uphold, and explain them for others is to let words and letters flow forth from the light of Prajñā, proclaiming them on behalf of the Buddha;
this is not comparable to the mere words displayed on paper or the interpretation of meaning based solely on the text. This is able to abide nowhere...
One who practices giving while in accordance with the Dharma attains merit superior to that;

namely, the merit naturally and inherently possessed within the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*—even a single four-line sublime verse—which encompasses all sentient beings throughout the realms of body and sense-faculties as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All are contained within the merit of the Tathāgata; they are vastly superior to those who practice giving while manifesting in physical form.
Subhūti, to speak in brief, this sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
The Tathāgata has taught it for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle. If there is anyone...
Those who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this to others—the Tathāgata fully knows these people and fully sees these people;
they all achieve immeasurable, incomparable, boundless, and inconceivable merit.
Such persons as these carry upon their shoulders the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Subhūti, those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span;
they will therefore be unable to hear, receive, read, recite, or explain this sutra to others.
This essential statement conveys the purport of the entire Sūtra. It transcends ordinary sentiments and worldly views;
therefore, it is inconceivable. It transcends language and written characters; therefore, it is beyond discussion. It transcends calculation and reckoning; therefore, it is immeasurable.
It fills the ten directions and pervades the three realms; therefore, it is boundless. As for what is called its merit—
This virtue is precisely that which was previously described as giving without dwelling upon signs. This is the ultimate pinnacle of the Buddha-dharma;
it is not something that those of inferior faculties or small capacities can uphold. The Tathāgata has taught this specifically for those of the Bodhisattva vehicle and the Buddha vehicle.
One who is able to give rise to the Mahāyāna mind is a bodhisattva; one who gives rise to the mind of the Supreme Vehicle is identical to a Tathāgata.
This unsurpassed Dharma-gate requires someone to shoulder its burden. If one fears the great and clings to the small, one will certainly be unable to bear the responsibility.
This is what is meant in Confucianism by the saying: "It is man who can propagate the Way; it is not the Way that propagates man. Furthermore—
To state further: those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and expound these merits shall possess the knowledge and vision of a Buddha;

they shall be protected and remembered by the Tathāgata and entrusted with his charge. They shall accomplish a treasury of great merit and bear it upon one shoulder, never retreating from unsurpassed bodhi.
However, those who delight in inferior dharmas will willingly settle for the lowly and become attached to a self.
They perceive [a self] and, having discriminated it, they become attached to the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*).

They exclude the four modes of birth from the scope of liberation and hope for the prolongation of their physical life, thereby becoming attached to the views of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*) and a life-principle (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*). These four views persist in the hidden and subtle;

these four characteristics accumulate as arising and ceasing. Thus, they are unable to accord with the purport of this sutra, nor can they believe, accept, read, recite, or explain it to others, as has been described above.
Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra may be found, it should be honored by all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras.
You should know that such a place is itself a stupa; everyone should pay homage, prostrate, and circumambulate it with reverence.
They scattered various flowers and incense upon that place.

This praises the fact that the Dharma-body of Prajñā is eternally abiding. Worldly people merely know to revere and have faith in the Dharma-jewel, yet they do not realize that the Dharma-jewel is itself the Dharma-body.
It is the locus where the life of wisdom of all Buddhas of the three periods of time is entrusted; it is the nature of all sentient beings.
Life itself depends upon this. Everywhere and in every place there is this Dharma-treasure; everywhere and in every place there is this Dharma-body.
Devas, humans, and asuras alike possess it and share in it; it is that which should be honored.

After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, his śarīra relics and true body were left behind, for which stupas were erected and adorned in the heavens and among men—this is indeed an act of reverence. This sutra is...
The Tathāgata’s bequeathed teaching consists of his own direct words; it is not comparable to ordinary written texts.
Those who should reverently circumambulate that place and scatter flowers and incense there do so because reverence signifies taking refuge, and circumambulation signifies dedication of merit.
The scattering of flowers and incense represents all merits that adorn the Buddha-lands; it is thus everywhere, for there is nothing that is not Prajñā.
Furthermore, Subhūti, if good men and good women receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, and if for the sake of others...

If this person is despised by others, their karmic offenses from previous lives—which would otherwise cause them to fall into the evil realms—are immediately extinguished because of this present-world contempt. They shall thereby attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This praises the merit of *prajñā*. It possesses the benefit of removing obstacles and emerging from the entanglements. Previously, the cultivation of wholesome qualities was explained;
now, the elimination of evil is explained. Regarding those who have committed determinate karma (*niyata-karma*) that cannot be avoided:

by cultivating the cause of *prajñā*, the sinful karma of previous lives that would otherwise lead to rebirth in the three evil realms is transformed from heavy to light through the power of *prajñā*, such that it does not exceed the duration of residual karmic fruition.
[Response: Determined karma is difficult to escape; one will be treated with contempt by others.
However, upon entering the gate of Prajñā, the karmic offenses of previous lives are immediately eliminated, and one attains unsurpassed Bodhi.

This treatise was composed because there are those in the world who have faith and practice goodness—those who believe in the sutras and cultivate their nature—who, despite their present hardships, suffer humiliation regarding status and position, and endure difficulties in food and clothing.
It is difficult. Those who have endured insults, abuse, and contempt are likewise not few. To the worldly eye, this leads them to claim that the Buddha-dharma lacks efficacy.
Yet they do not realize that this very contempt is precisely the cause for transformation and the occasion for swiftly attaining unsurpassed Bodhi;
one must not, because of this, become discouraged or retreat. The Buddha spoke these words to Śūnyatā-utpatti (Kōshō) to proclaim this.
"Subhūti, I recall that in the past, during immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas before the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara,
I encountered eight hundred and forty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas, all of whom I served and made offerings to, never letting any pass in vain."

Furthermore, Subhūti, if there should be someone who, in the final age at the end of time, is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, the merit they obtain shall not be equaled by the merit of my own offerings to all the Buddhas—even a hundredth part, a thousandth, ten-thousandth, a hundred-thousandth, a millionth, ten-millionth, a hundred-millionth, a billionth, or even a trillionth part;
it cannot be reached by calculation or by any analogy. Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family, in the future...
In the final age, should there be those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, if I were to fully describe the merit they would obtain,
some upon hearing it might have their minds become deranged and, filled with doubt, fail to believe. Subhūti, you should know that the meaning of this sutra is inconceivable,
and its karmic fruit and retribution are likewise inconceivable.

This is the Tathāgata manifesting his body and preaching the Dharma. He speaks in the highest terms of the supreme cause that is *prajñā*, stating that it cannot be equaled by making offerings to or serving all the Buddhas.

He reflects: "In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I encountered countless hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas, such as Dīpaṃkara Buddha, and I made offerings to and served them all without fail."
This kind of merit is truly not comparable to the aforementioned sacrifice of body and life.

Furthermore, if there were another person in the final age who recites the merits of this sutra, their merit would surpass that of my own service and offerings; my merit would not equal even one hundredth of theirs.
Even that which cannot be reached by numerous equal portions—this refers to the fact that signless merit surpasses conditioned phenomena by a factor of ten thousand times ten thousand.
To speak to the utmost regarding the merit of this sutra, it is thus inconceivable. Its merit is inexhaustible; I say it is inexhaustible.
Sentient beings are inexhaustible; doubt and faith are inexhaustible. The Tathāgata accords with their faculties.
Though they are vessels [of the Dharma], one must skillfully guide them. It cannot be left unsaid, yet it cannot be fully explained. This is what is meant by: "Stop, stop; there is no need to speak.

My Dharma is subtle and inconceivable. To exhaustively convey it in a single phrase would cause hearers to easily give rise to doubt, their minds becoming deranged and confused, leading them instead to slander and fall into the three evil realms. What would benefit them would thus actually harm them. This gives rise to the following passage.
Regarding the intent of Subhūti’s repeated question:

at that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, how should a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds? The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Bodhi. Sons of good family, daughters of good family, those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should give rise to this thought:
'I shall bring all sentient beings to liberation; having brought all sentient beings to liberation, [I shall remain in the world until the task is complete]'."
Yet there is not a single sentient being who has been truly brought to parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.
And why is that? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma whatsoever by which one sets out for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This section of questions and answers involves some degree of redundancy. *Hanshan Jueyi* (Hanshan’s Decisions on Doubts) states briefly:

From the initial question regarding "abiding" and "subduing" onwards, [the text] generally refutes the doubts held by ordinary beings who practice as bodhisattvas. One should know that the two types of grasping—grasping at a self (*ātman*) and grasping at phenomena (*dharma*)—have both coarse and subtle levels.
The preceding [section] refuted the coarse grasping of ordinary beings, using the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and form (*rūpa*) as the objects of their grasping.
Taking the self as the object of grasping (*ātma-grāha*) and taking that which is the basis of the self as the object-condition (*ālambana-viṣaya*) constitutes the grasping of a self.

The practice of the six perfections by one who seeks enlightenment constitutes the grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). Because both of these graspings rely on such objects and are thus attachments to signs (*nimitta*), they are refuted.

This is to resolve the doubts of a bodhisattva at the stage of initial resolve who has not yet realized Prajñāpāramitā; it merely demonstrates that, from a lower perspective, there are no sentient beings to be saved. This...
Subsequently, one breaks through the subtle dual attachments to self and dharmas; such a person is a bodhisattva who has already awakened to prajñā.
Yet, they still cling to the wisdom that realizes as "self" and the true thusness (tathatā) that is realized as "person. This constitutes the capacity to realize and the capacity to awaken.
For the sake of sentient beings, their realization remains unforgetting and continues secretly as if it were their very life; thus they act as "those who possess longevity.
Because these four characteristics are most extremely subtle, they constitute the two subtle types of grasping—namely, the persistence of the notion of self and the awareness of a self.

Therefore, what follows below develops this by singling out the single word "self," thereby exclusively refuting the grasping at a self, such that one no longer perceives above there to be a fruit of Buddhahood to be sought.

This is similar to the preceding text, though the question is the same while the meaning differs; the observer should understand this. Regarding the initial questions in the Sūtra—“How should one dwell?

How should one subdue the mind?”—these refer to the bodhisattva at the first stage, an ordinary person with a great resolve who has just begun to give rise to the mind of saving sentient beings, yet still possesses various attachments to signs and practices based on attachment to their own five aggregates and physical body.
Regarding their practice of giving, they seek karmic rewards while clinging to the coarse characteristics of the six sense objects.
Regarding the bodhi they seek, they cling to the physical form of the transformation Buddha. Their land is a land adorned with various jewels.
All their diverse practices do not transcend these signs; thus, they are far removed from Prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti raises this question, which is addressed by the Buddha in successive layers.
Refutation: Only when all marks of form (*rūpa*) are completely transcended does one accord with *tathatā* (suchness).

When the true wisdom of *prajñā* reaches this point, Śūnyatā-janman has attained awakening and the doubts of the great assembly have been dispelled. All preceding passages in the sutra prior to the words "inconceivable" (*acintya*) convey this same meaning.
From this point in the sutra onward, however, it refutes those bodhisattvas who have already awakened to *prajñā* yet remain subtle [in their understanding].
Regarding subtle attachments: the four marks are all subtle. Upon reaching this point, [the text] singles out the single character "I" (ātman) as the primary focus, stating only:

"I should bring sentient beings to extinction. It no longer mentions giving (dāna). From this, we know that the Bodhisattva has already attained awakening and their meritorious practices are complete;
there remains only the view of "sentient being" and "Buddha" that has not yet been extinguished. Furthermore, this subtle wisdom takes "I" as its object. Moreover—
Question: Why is it that this inquiry regarding "abiding in subjugation" (praśamana) appears to have the same intent as the previous question? Answer:

It is because this Bodhisattva, having already detached from the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), yet has not yet forgotten their habitual tendencies (vāsanā). Consequently, within the wisdom of True Suchness (tathatā-jñāna), they still seek a place of abiding.

Furthermore, thinking that there must be a locus where enlightenment (bodhi) resides, they seek it but cannot find it, which causes their mind to become unsettled; thus, they inquire about subjugation. This is why.
The aspiration for Buddhahood is not yet settled because the view of a distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas has not been extinguished;
failing to realize the principle of equality and suchness, one asks as if the meaning were the same while the referents were different. Therefore, the World-Honored One refutes this, saying:
"One who has resolved upon Bodhicitta should contemplate in this way: 'After I have brought all sentient beings to nirvāṇa, in reality, not a single sentient being has attained nirvāṇa.'"
This is because sentient beings are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*); they do not require further extinction or further deliverance.

If one clings to the existence of extinction and deliverance, one becomes attached to the four marks and is no longer a bodhisattva. Thus, it is not seen that there are sentient beings who can be delivered.
Since the living and the Buddha are originally equal, and since sentient beings cannot be extinguished, there is truly no dharma within this to be sought.
As for bodhi: why is this? Because sentient beings are fundamentally quiescent from the very beginning; this is itself bodhi.
One need not seek it further; one does not perceive that there is any fruit of Buddhahood to be sought.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata, while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma called 'anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi'?

"No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there was no dharma that the Buddha obtained as 'anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi' while with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. The Buddha said, "So it is..."
"So it is, Subhūti; so it is. In truth, there is no dharma by which the Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Subhūti, if there were any dharma by which the Tathāgata had attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed upon me this prediction: 'In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni.'"
Śākyamuni. There is, in truth, no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For this reason, Dīpaṃkara Buddha conferred upon me the prediction, saying: "In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni. Why is this?
Because "Tathāgata" is precisely the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas. If someone were to say that the Tathāgata...
[He] attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Subhūti, regarding this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata, therein there is neither reality nor unreality. Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all dharmas are...
"This is the Buddha-dharma, Subhūti. As for what is called 'all dharmas,' they are not all dharmas; therefore they are called 'all dharmas.
This follows from the preceding statement that in unsurpassed enlightenment there is truly no dharma to be attained. The Buddha then addressed Subhūti.
He then questioned him further: "In the past, you received a prediction from Dīpaṃkara Buddha; everyone then said that there is a dharma to be attained in unsurpassed bodhi.

Subhūti, having attained realization, understood the wondrous meaning of what the Buddha had taught and came to know with certainty that there is no dharma to be attained in unsurpassed bodhi—this is called true attainment. The Buddha confirmed this, saying, "So it is, so it is. This is what is meant.
This means that only when there is truly no dharma to be attained is it the ultimate pinnacle of unsurpassed bodhi.

Because of this, when Dīpaṃkara bestowed his prediction that I would attain Buddhahood, had I truly possessed any attainment regarding the dharma, I would not have been named Tathāgata, nor would I have received that prediction.
Thus, he repeatedly clarified the meaning of the non-attainment of any dharma. The Tathāgata—
Regarding the prophecy that one shall become Śākyamuni: the "Tathāgata" (如來) is one of the ten titles [of a Buddha].

Such is the meaning of the term *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), namely the essence of *tathatā* (suchness). Because it is without gain or loss, and without coming or going, it is called "Tathāgata.
When the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood, Dīpaṃkara bestowed this prophecy upon him; this is precisely this meaning, and there is nothing further to it.

It is attained. Yet, if there were another person who said, "Unsurpassed Bodhi is truly something that can be attained," they would not realize that there is no dharma whatsoever that can be attained;
this is called true attainment. Being neither real nor false, it is called truly having nothing to attain.
All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are precisely the wondrous truth that is neither real nor unreal.
Whether they are dharmas or non-dharmas, they are all called "Buddha-dharma. To speak of it in essence: what is called Buddha-dharma is itself not Buddha-dharma. An ancient worthy said:

"When functioning, one knows while remaining eternally quiescent; when not functioning, one is quiescent while remaining eternally knowing. Only then does one accord with wondrous enlightenment. This is so.
Therefore, they are called "all dharmas.
Subhūti, it is like a person’s body being tall and large. Subhūti said, "World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body being tall and large, that is precisely not a large body;
it is merely named a 'large body. Subhūti, a bodhisattva is also like this. If...
If one speaks thus, saying, "I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to final nirvāṇa," that person is not called a bodhisattva.

Why is this? Subhūti, in reality there is no dharma that can be named a bodhisattva. Therefore, the Buddha has said that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to speak thus, "I shall adorn..."
"Buddha-field. One is not called a bodhisattva for this reason. Why? The Tathāgata has said that what is called the adornment of a Buddha-field is in fact no adornment;
it is only called "adornment" [by way of designation]. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva penetrates the dharma of non-self, the Tathāgata says that such a person is truly a bodhisattva.
This borrowing of a "great body" serves as a metaphor for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); it must not be sought through attachment to signs.
When the Tathāgata questioned him, Subhūti attained realization: apart from the great body, there is a "non-body," and this non-body is the Dharma-body.
If a bodhisattva maintains self-clinging—thinking "I shall deliver sentient beings"—they are still grasping at the great body as the self and no longer know [the true nature].
If there were a true self, one would not be called a bodhisattva. Why is this? In reality, there is no dharma that can be named "bodhisattva.
There is no great body; this is called "non-body. Dharma is non-dharma; body is non-body.
Marks are themselves non-marks. The self, persons, sentient beings, and life-span all return to nothingness; how could there be any further dharma to be obtained?
Furthermore, taking the Buddha-field as a metaphor: the Buddha-field is the field of the mind. Since the Buddha-field is without marks, how can it be adorned?
If there were anything to be adorned, that would mean there is a dharma to be obtained, and it could not be called [the Buddha-field].
Bodhisattva, you should know that what the Tathāgata calls "adornment" is the adornment of the Dharma-body, not the adornment of the great physical body.
The Dharma-body is no-body. To realize that it is no-body is called adornment;
to penetrate the dharma of non-self such that not a single dharma can be apprehended—this is what is called a true Bodhisattva.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye? "Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye? "Yes, [World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye]."
“Venerable One, the Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
“Yes, World-Honored One, the Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye. “Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding the Ganges River...”
"Are all the grains of sand therein, Subhūti, what the Buddha calls 'sand'? " "Yes, World-Honored One; the Tathāgata calls them sand.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River."
“Subhūti, suppose there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; would they be many? “Very many, World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Subhūti: “In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings.
Why is this? The Tathāgata has said that all minds are ‘no-minds’; it is for this reason they are called ‘minds. And why is that, Subhūti?”
"Bodhi. The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended. This follows from the preceding text.
After the Bodhisattva has attained awakening, subtle attachments to persons and phenomena (pudgala-dharma) still remain.
Among all characteristics, the Buddha uniquely singles out the "self" (ātman), and within that characteristic of self, he reveals the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Furthermore, it says:
It is not the body. Through various refutations, it is shown that there is no dharma to be grasped.

Yet, fearing that the Bodhisattva’s profound faith in the signless understanding might cause him to sink into emptiness, stagnate in stillness, and fall into the attachment to emptiness—thereby remaining subject to partiality and deficiency—the Buddha calls out to Subhūti to interrogate him.
He enumerates the five eyes to verify the previous understanding, pointing to his own present blue-lotus-colored eyes as proof. These are the very eyes of the Tathāgata.
That which is on the face is the flesh eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). That which sees the various heavens above and penetrates down to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) below is the heavenly eye (*divya-cakṣus*).

That which illuminates and perceives the depth and shallowness of the faculties and natures of sentient beings, as well as their transmigration within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), is the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*). That which illuminates and perceives the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the Dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*).
That which pervades the entire Dharma-realm and discriminates between all that exists and does not exist, as well as the empty and the provisional, is the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).

That which illuminates and beholds the Buddha-lands and boundless worlds, emitting light universally to shatter all darkness and perfecting the ten directions without obstruction or hindrance, is the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*).
The fleshly eye belongs to the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) of the Tathāgata; the four kinds of noble eyes belong to the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
The pure Dharma-body is formless; yet without relying on the Reward-body, it cannot deliver sentient beings. The noble eye is formless;
yet without relying on the fleshly eye, it cannot perceive objects. If one insists that it is definitively non-existent, one falls into the nihilism of the external paths.

Therefore, [the Buddha] enumerated the five eyes one by one to interrogate him. Subhūti, having attained realization, answered the questions according to the occasion without giving rise to conceptual understanding.

The Tathāgata again used the sands of the Ganges as a metaphor; Subhūti believed they were exceedingly numerous, whereupon the Tathāgata enlightened him regarding the scope of the minds of sentient beings—that which the Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees is due to the possession of the five eyes.
The ultimate measure of the sentient beings' mental scope is manifold and diverse in its myriad distinctions; it all belongs to deluded thought and is entirely not the true mind.
That which is "not-mind" is precisely what is called "mind. It is like the physical eye, which serves as the locus for the noble eye (the divine eye), and is thus called "an eye.

Furthermore, fearing that upon hearing these teachings on various minds one might assume there is a substantial, real mind, it must be further refuted and eliminated. This has already been done in the past.
The past has ceased; the present is illusory; the future has not yet arisen. When sought through investigation across these three time periods, the mind cannot be found at all.
What is seen by the five eyes is, in a flash, realized as emptiness; both existence and non-existence are thereby dispelled.

"Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this cause, acquire much merit? "So it is, World-Honored One.
That person, by reason of this cause, would acquire very much merit. "Subhūti, if merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one acquires it."
The merit is great. Because there is no merit, the Tathāgata says that one obtains great merit.
Although the sūtras repeatedly speak of the retribution of merit, it seems unnecessary to mention it once a bodhisattva has already attained awakening.

That the Tathāgata questions and examines them again and again is likely out of concern that even bodhisattvas who have already awakened may still harbor subtle attachments regarding persons and phenomena.
Not yet forgetting the view of cultivating merit remains a matter of attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*). It must be repeatedly refuted and discarded. "Existence" refers to grasping at signs;
"non-existence" refers to being free from signs. To see the nature by being free from signs—that nature is like empty space—its merit is immeasurable.
Compared to what was previously explained regarding upholding, reciting, and expounding, this goes one level deeper.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Buddha be seen by means of his physical body (*rūpakāya*)? "No, World-Honored One."
The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the body of perfected form. Why is this?
The Tathāgata has said that the body of perfected form is itself not a body of perfected form; it is merely designated as "the body of perfected form. Subhūti, what do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the possession of the various marks? "No, World-Honored One. The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the possession of..."

[The Buddha spoke of] "the perception of various marks. Why is this? The Tathāgata has said: "To be fully endowed with various marks is precisely not to be fully endowed; it is called being fully endowed with various marks.
The preceding passage clears away the perception of marks, such that one must neither grasp at existence nor fall into emptiness. Yet, there remains a fear that the Bodhisattva [might still do so].
Having attained awakening, he gave rise to doubt, thinking: "The merit of giving is the cause for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it brings about the fruit of being endowed with perfect adornments.
Now, you say that merit is truly non-existent, which means there is no fruit. There is no Buddha to be attained, which also means there is no fruit.
Yet, how is it that the Tathāgata appears in this very body, fully endowed with physical marks? Thus he called out:

Śūnyatā-utpanna (Kōshō) was questioned and examined; at the moment of these words, he attained realization. He said that one should not perceive the Tathāgata through the various marks of the physical body (*rūpakāya*).

This is because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of conduct, and it is for this reason that this Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is formed, being fully endowed with the thirty-two primary marks. Once the Dharma-body is recognized, one should no longer rely upon the Reward-body.

This is a view that arises within one's own body. Furthermore, you should personally realize and awaken to the fact that what the Tathāgata described as the "body of form endowed with all attributes" is nothing other than this illusory physical frame within this mass of flesh. You should know that within it dwells a single True Person of No Station.
The pure and wondrously colored body is what is called the Dharma-body; therefore, it is said that it is "not a body of complete form.
This "is not" is precisely "is. To possess all marks means to be adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics and myriad virtues, which goes beyond merely the thirty-two primary marks.
Furthermore, upon being questioned and examined, Subhūti attained realization, exactly as explained previously, saying:
To be "endowed with all marks" refers to the physical body as it was in accordance with past retribution; therefore, it is said that this is "not truly endowed.
To be "separated from all marks" means that the Tathāgata cannot be seen [in such a way]; therefore, it is said that this is "called being endowed."
Subhūti, do not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall teach some dharma. Do not have such a thought. Why is that?
If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata has taught some dharma, they would be slandering the Buddha, for they would not understand what I have taught.
Subhūti, as for one who teaches the Dharma, there is no dharma that can be taught; it is merely called "teaching the Dharma."
Continuing from the preceding passage: The wondrous marks are markless; they certainly cannot be seen through various characteristics.

Even this present preaching of the Dharma is the teaching of non-teaching; it cannot be sought through verbal expression. Speaking to Subhūti: that the Tathāgata’s various marks are not marks is indeed so.
Regarding this present preaching of the Dharma, one must not cling to marks. Do not say that the Tathāgata transcends the mind.
One should form this thought: "I shall preach the Dharma. Yet the preacher does not form this thought, nor should the listener form such a thought.
If a person gains understanding from these words and claims that the Tathāgata has preached the Dharma, they do not have faith in the Buddha;
rather, they have faith in all Buddhas. Why is this? Because the Dharma I have preached does not reside in words.
He said: "Those who are attached to signs take only the verbal expression as the teaching; they are unable to understand my 'teaching of non-teaching.
He further addressed Subhūti to clarify this, saying: 'In all cases of preaching the Dharma, fundamentally there is no dharma that can be preached.
It is only for the sake of removing the external delusions of sentient beings that one preaches. Thus, delusion is used to dispel delusion; there is nothing truly real.'"
Once one has attained awakening, this method is no longer required.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings in future ages who..."
"Upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will they give rise to faith? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, they are not sentient beings, yet they are not non-sentient beings.
Why is this? Subhūti, those who are called 'sentient beings' have been described by the Tathāgata as non-sentient beings; it is merely a designation for 'sentient beings.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, has the Buddha attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
"Is it because there is nothing to be attained? The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti.
In my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be attained;
this is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, Subhūti, this dharma is equal, without high or low; this is called..."
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is attained by practicing all wholesome dharmas while being without a self, without a person, without a sentient being, and without a life-span.
Subhūti, as for what are called "wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata says they are not wholesome dharmas; they are merely designated as "wholesome dharmas."
Continuing from the preceding text: "There is no dharma that can be taught; this is called teaching the Dharma.

Subhūti attained the wondrous realization of the *dharmakāya* and was thus able to believe, accept, and continue the Buddha’s life of wisdom. For this reason, he is at that time called "Subhūti, the Life of Wisdom" (*prajñājīvita*).
This demonstrates that the arising of phenomena and the Dharma are one and the same; there is no dharma that can be spoken of, and no sentient beings who can be saved.

When Kūṇapa (Empty Birth) realized the principle that there is no dharma that can be spoken of, he feared that future sentient beings, upon hearing this wondrous Dharma, might not know whether they could believe and accept it, and so he questioned the Buddha.
He received the answer: "If one forms such an understanding, this itself is the Buddha-dharma of sentient beings."
It is divided into two parts. One should know that sentient beings are fundamentally suchness (*tathatā*) and equal to the Dharma;
they possess no marks of a "sentient being. Therefore, it is said: "They are not sentient beings. Yet, because true suchness follows conditions to manifest as sentient beings, it is said:
"It is not that they are not sentient beings. Furthermore, he speaks to Śūnyatā-utpanna (Kūṣi) to clarify the reason for this: what is called a "sentient being" refers to...
I preach all dharmas for the sake of delivering all sentient beings. Since there are no sentient beings, there are no dharmas.
Dharmas give rise to sentient beings, and sentient beings give rise to dharmas; this is what is called "the birth of sentient beings.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says they are not sentient beings, yet they are named "sentient beings. The thought of emptiness holds that the Buddha-dharma depends upon sentient beings.
Only then would there be a dharma; yet, since nothing is to be attained, is the unsurpassed *bodhi* attained by the Buddha now something that exists or something that does not exist?
The Buddha determined it to be non-existent and thus confirmed it, saying to Subhūti:

"The unsurpassed *bodhi*, I and all sentient beings equally possess its true nature (*dharmatā*). Fundamentally, there is neither gain nor loss. That there is nothing to be attained is indeed so. Thus he spoke.
All subtle and minute dharmas are entirely unattainable; for this reason, it is called unsurpassed bodhi. He further addressed them, saying:
"That which is called 'dharma' is the dharma of the equal and perfect enlightenment of all sentient beings.
To awaken to it is to be a Buddha, yet there is no mark of superiority. To be deluded by it is to be a sentient being, yet there is no mark of inferiority. Therefore, it is so named."
This is for the sake of unsurpassed bodhi. If one clings to the marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, then it is not equanimity.
By relinquishing these four marks and cultivating all wholesome dharmas, one attains unsurpassed bodhi. As for "wholesome dharmas," these refer to what is described in the sūtra:
giving, making offerings, paying homage, adorning the buddha-lands, and so forth; all such things are called wholesome.
Dharmas are also called conditioned dharmas; therefore, it is said that what is not a wholesome dharma is called a wholesome dharma.

Subhūti, if someone were to take all the Sumeru kings of mountains within a trichiliocosm and offer such a heap of the seven treasures as a gift, yet another person were to take this Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra...
Even if one were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain to others even as little as a four-line verse [from this sutra], the previously mentioned merit would not equal a hundredth part of it;
nor a hundred-thousand-billionth part; nor could it be reached by any calculation, number, or analogy.

Continuing from the preceding text: since wholesome dharmas are thus negated, even the "jewel-heap" of giving is not a wholesome dharma; only the merit of *prajñā* (wisdom) can be called truly sublime.

This is because within the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, even a single four-line verse is the locus where the Tathāgata’s life of wisdom is entrusted, and it is the very pivot upon which the delusion and enlightenment of sentient beings depend. If one receives, upholds, recites, or explains [such verses]...
Such a person is then able to continue the Buddha’s life-force of wisdom and cause sentient beings to turn their backs on delusion and unite with awakening.
Their merit and virtue are so vast that they far exceed the gift of a heap of jewels; the difference between them is immense.
Subhūti, what do you think? You should not think that the Tathāgata has this thought: "I shall deliver sentient beings.
Subhūti, do not have such a thought. Why is that? Because, in reality, there are no sentient beings whom the Tathāgata delivers.
If there were any sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, then the Tathāgata would possess a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Subhūti, when the Tathāgata says that there is a self, it is not actually a self; yet ordinary people imagine that there is a self.
Subhūti, those who are called "ordinary persons" by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, ordinary persons; they are merely designated as "ordinary persons.
As stated in the preceding passage: to expound even four lines of verse from this sutra for others constitutes the merit of saving sentient beings.
Fearing that people might misunderstand and think that the Tathāgata has a deliberate intention regarding the deliverance of sentient beings, he addressed Subhūti to clarify this, saying:

"Do not say that the Tathāgata forms a thought to deliver sentient beings; you too should not harbor such a thought, thinking that the Tathāgata truly possesses the mark of delivering sentient beings.
If there were any sentient beings delivered by the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata would [be one who delivers them]."

If there were a self that could deliver others, and persons who were delivered—such that these persons and sentient beings were regarded as a "self" or a "life-principle"—then this would not be the true self of a Tathāgata.
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, in reality there is no such self; yet ordinary people [perceive it otherwise].
From birth, people conceive of a self and believe that a self exists; consequently, they come to suspect that the Tathāgata likewise possesses a self.
In truth, this Dharma is equal, without high or low. To awaken to it is to be a sage; to be deluded by it is to be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Though called an "ordinary person," he is not actually an ordinary person; yet he is designated as such because, within the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), there is neither sage nor ordinary person.
"It is so, Subhūti.
What do you think? Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks? Subhūti said, "So it is, so it is.
The Tathāgata can be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks. The Buddha said, "Subhūti, if one [perceives him]..."
Regarding those who perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks: a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) would thus be the Tathāgata. Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, one should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks."
This refers back distantly to the "complete physical marks. The thirty-two marks constitute the complete physical marks.

Following the preceding explanation regarding the saving of sentient beings, there is a sincere concern that sentient beings might give rise to doubt, thinking that the Buddha manifests a body and preaches the Dharma.
It is not separate from the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). The body belongs to the realm of form and appearance, while the Dharma consists of sound.

If one were to set aside both form and sound, from what would the Dharma be preached, and by what means could it be heard? Subhūti was called by name and thus interrogated; Subhūti was able to respond with conviction.
He attained realization upon hearing these words: "The Tathāgata cannot be perceived by means of physical marks.

The Buddha again cited the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) to substantiate this point, for even though the Universal Monarch also possesses these thirty-two marks, he remains an ordinary person and cannot be called a Tathāgata.
Subhūti reiterated his previous realization, stating that the Tathāgata cannot...
Regarding those who observe by means of marks: it is precisely the markless that is the Tathāgata; he cannot be seen through form, nor can he be sought through sound.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: "If one sees me by means of form, or seeks me by means of sound, such a person..."
They follow false paths and are unable to see the Tathāgata.

According to the four-line verse in the sutra, it appears to refer to these very four lines. Since there is not a single word "verse" (gāthā) within the sutra itself, the explicit mention of a "verse" here clearly indicates that the commentary must pertain to this.
One should know that this verse is none other than the preceding text [which lacks the word "verse"].
The four phrases—self, person, sentient being, and life-span—are the initial designation of names and characteristics. This verse, however, sweeps away erroneous interpretations.

Those who practice erroneously are precisely sentient beings attached to signs; from the side of form and sound, they perversely give rise to views such as "person" and "self," failing to see the self-nature of True Suchness (Tathāgata).
Thus, they do not see the Tathāgata who is presently preaching the Dharma before them.
Furthermore, when you taste these two instances of the word "self," you should recognize the true self; that is the "self" among the four virtues of the Tathāgata—permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Subhūti, if you should think that the Tathāgata does not attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi because he does not possess the marks of physical perfection...
[He] attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Subhūti, do not have this thought: that the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the possession of marks.
Subhūti, if you should have this thought—that those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* preach the annihilation and cessation of all phenomena—do not have such a thought.
Why is this? Those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena.
Although the preceding prose has already explained the verse, there is a concern that bodhisattvas, after their realization, might give rise to doubt, thinking: "The Tathāgata cannot..."
One perceives through form; one cannot seek [the Tathāgata] through sound. As stated in the sūtras:
"The Tathāgata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Apart from form and sound, who is it that attains? Is this not the cessation of all marks?
"And as for unsurpassed Bodhi, would it not likewise return to extinction? Is this indeed the ultimate?
Subhūti, these words of yours are entirely a matter of repeated and earnest admonition; they must not be understood as implying annihilation.
While it is certainly not the case that one attains Bodhi by means of signs of fullness, it is also not a form of annihilation to say that one does not attain Bodhi by means of signs of fullness.
See! You should know that supreme bodhi is fundamentally without cessation. Teaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings is entirely for the purpose of eliminating the four marks;
it never instructs people such that both [the teaching] and supreme bodhi would together return to cessation.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva were to take the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and give them as a gift, and if another person were to know that all dharmas are without self and thereby attain patience (*kṣānti*), this bodhisattva would surpass the merit obtained by the former bodhisattva. Why is this? Subhūti, it is because bodhisattvas do not accept merit.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, why does a bodhisattva not accept merit?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti, the merit performed by a bodhisattva should not be clung to with craving; for this reason, it is said that they do not accept merit.”
In the sutras, it is frequently stated that there are rewards for merit—whether shallow or deep, coarse or subtle—in countless instances.
All of these are because the Tathāgata skillfully observes the mental capacities of sentient beings. It is natural, indeed, for ordinary people to seek merit by clinging to signs.

These are the bodhisattvas of great resolve. Before they have attained realization and entry [into the truth], they cannot yet avoid frequently giving rise to views regarding karmic rewards based on their attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Once the bodhisattva has realized [the truth], their coarse attachments to persons and phenomena have already been forgotten;

yet, subtle attachments to phenomena still remain and have not been fully transformed. Thus, they diligently and zealously practice the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) and further exhort others to do the same.

In practicing giving, there still remains a subtle and minute view of receiving the retribution of blessings; therefore, when the sutra reaches this point, it reiterates and clarifies this by stating the two characters "one does not receive" (*a-pratigṛhṇāti*).
This means that if the retribution of blessings were non-existent, there would certainly be nothing to receive;

yet if the retribution of blessings were existent, it likewise could not be received. The three spheres are empty in essence, and the four marks are entirely absent; thus one thoroughly realizes all things.
All phenomena are without self. One achieves the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). All meritorious rewards are ultimately unobtainable;
there is no giver, nor is there any receiver. The world is empty; the seven treasures are empty; both the donor and the gift are empty.
Whether one accepts or does not accept [the merit], both are ultimately unattainable. Reaching this point is precisely the ultimate limit of meritorious retribution.
As for receiving, upholding, reciting, and expounding the sutra verses, it needs no further explanation. Subhūti further feared that Bodhisattvas might cling to dharmas;
therefore, as the Buddha taught, one must not accept merit. Only by completely relinquishing and utterly abandoning all merit does one become a Bodhisattva.
This would sever the worldly people’s inclination to cultivate merit; therefore, this question was asked. The Tathāgata explained it, saying:
"What is called 'not receiving' means that at the very moment one is performing a meritorious act, one does not give rise to even a single thought of greedy seeking or attachment to signs.
This is what is meant by 'not receiving. This is precisely what the Sixth Patriarch meant when he said: "Do not think of good; do not think of evil. The First Patriarch...
It says: "Giving is fundamentally without merit"—this is precisely that meaning.

Subhūti, if anyone were to say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, that person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught. Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. Therefore...
This is called "the Tathāgata.
Following the preceding text, it states that he does not receive merit. This is because one might harbor doubts, thinking:

"The Tathāgata of the present time moves with mastery through the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining; is this not one who accepts and receives blessings and virtues? Therefore, [it is clarified].
He called out to Subhūti to enlighten him, saying: "If you hold such a view, you do not understand the meaning of what I previously taught regarding the non-appropriation of merit.
For it is said that 'Tathāgata' is the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
Although one speaks of 'coming,' there is nowhere from which he comes; although one speaks of 'going,' there is nowhere to which he goes. There is no going, and no cessation."
That which comes not and is not born is the true Buddha of self-nature; it possesses no merit that can be received.
Subhūti, if a good man or a good woman were to grind the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system into fine dust, what do you think?
Would that mass of atoms be numerous? Subhūti said: "It would be very many, World-Honored One."
World-Honored One, why is this? If these multitudes of atoms were truly existent, the Buddha would not have called them "multitudes of atoms.
Why is that? The Buddha said: "The multitudes of atoms are not, in fact, multitudes of atoms; they are merely named 'multitudes of atoms.
World-Honored One, as for the so-called "trichiliocosm" spoken of by the Tathāgata, it is not, in fact, a world; it is merely named a "world. Why is this?
For this reason, Subhūti, if a world-realm were truly existent, it would be a "single unified mass. The Tathāgata has said that what is a single unified mass is not a single unified mass;
it is merely called a "single unified mass. Subhūti, that which is a single unified mass is ineffable;
yet ordinary people greedily cling to such things.

Continuing from above, it is said that there is nowhere from which [the Buddha] comes and nowhere to which he goes; this means that the Buddha-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm, manifesting in harmonious union wherever it may be.
Suppose one were to grind the world into fine dust; even when the Buddha unites with these particles, he does not become more numerous—this is what is meant by "the great merging into the small.
Conversely, suppose one were to gather those fine dust particles back into a world; even when the Buddha merges with that world, [he does not become less].
It is not "great," for it refers to the merging of the small into the great. Ultimately, the true nature of the Tathāgata is neither one nor two; there is no separation and no merging.
When merged with a minute particle (*paramāṇu*), there are realms within that particle; when merged with a world-system, there are particles within that realm.
Therefore, it is said to be neither a minute particle nor a world-system. When merged with a minute particle, there is a Buddha within that particle; when merged...
Within the world-systems, there are Buddhas; therefore, it is called "microdust" and it is called "world-system.
The first is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). "Union" refers to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). It is neither real nor empty, neither existent nor non-existent.

If one were to consider it as truly existent, this would mean the Dharma-body is united with the Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that this is the "single unified mark" (*ekaghanalakṣaṇa*) of the Dharma-realm.
Because it is distinct from the *dharmakāya*, it is said: "It is not a unified whole. Because the *dharmakāya* is not separate from the *dharmadhātu*, it is said:
"This is called a unified whole. Ultimately, both "is" and "is not" are ineffable; only the awakened one attains this. As for ordinary people, they cannot yet avoid greedy attachment;
they cling to principle and are hindered by phenomena, or they cling to phenomena and are hindered by principle. This is what is meant:
That which is a "unified mark" (ekapiṇḍalakṣaṇa) falls into the extreme of substantial phenomena; through craving, attachment, and clinging, one fails to attain mastery.

The Buddha spoke thus to Śūnyatā-utpāda (Subhūti), repeatedly elucidating this to resolve the subtle dual attachments to persons and dharmas that remain even after a Bodhisattva has attained awakening.
Subhūti, if someone were to say, "The Buddha has taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span," Subhūti, what do you think?
Would that person understand the meaning of what I have taught? "No, World-Honored One. That person would not understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught.
Why is this? Because the World-Honored One has said: 'The view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span...'"

To see them is not to have a view of a self, a view of a person, a view of a sentient being, or a view of a life-span. It is precisely these that are called the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.

Subhūti, those who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should, regarding all phenomena, know them thus, see them thus, and believe and understand them thus, so that they do not give rise to the notion of phenomena.
Subhūti, that which is called the "characteristic of dharmas" has been taught by the Tathāgata as not being a characteristic of dharmas;

it is merely designated as the "characteristic of dharmas. This connects back to the preceding passage: those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.
To provide a further interpretation: this refers to the sweeping away of subtle attachments to dharmas and cognitive views. The "inferior dharmas" mentioned previously are—
This was taught for those who delight in the Hīnayāna: they perceive a self characterized by the form and appearance of the five aggregates;

they perceive a person who stands in opposition to that self; they perceive sentient beings possessed of ignorance and afflictions; and they perceive a life-principle that remains embodied and dwells in the world.
Through various deluded views, one consequently forms various attachments to signs. To empty all signs, one must first empty all views;
only then will one not fall into the level of the Śrāvaka or the ordinary person.

When the sutra reaches this point, it is for the sake of Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas who have already entered the gate of awakening and no longer possess any signs of self, person, being, or life. However, within subtle delusions—

He possessed some degree of cognitive insight. He perceived the "self" that has already awakened, as well as those who have likewise awakened, sentient beings who have not yet awakened, and the "life-spanner" (jīvaka) who maintains the continuity of the life-force of wisdom after awakening. As long as this perception persists, one remains attached to what appears to be true vision;
thus, one cannot transcend directly and enter immediately to attain Bodhi. Therefore, he addressed Subhūti by name and questioned him, saying: "I previously..."
I have previously stated that the views of a self, a person, and so forth, were taught for those who delight in inferior dharmas.

If someone were to say, "The Tathāgata truly asserts a self," would this person understand the meaning of what I have taught? Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) realized this and understood with faith that such a person does not comprehend the subtle meaning of the Tathāgata.
Indeed, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he administers the medicine of the Dharma according to the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings.
For those who delight in inferior teachings, he destroys their false views and then explains various views; yet the views he explains are the views of sentient beings, not the views of the Buddha.
Because sentient beings possess these false views, he follows them according to the state into which they have fallen.
Yet these are merely termed "the view of a self," "the view of a person," "the view of a sentient being," and "the view of a life-span.
If a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva, having attained awakening, gives rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta, then all knowledge and views are simply all phenomena (*dharmas*).
To know in this way is true knowledge; to see in this way is true seeing; to believe in this way is true faith.
"Understanding" is precisely the dharma-gate of profound faith, understanding, and awakening; it does not give rise to further conceptual characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

For these conceptual characteristics, when attached to the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), are not true conceptual characteristics; only when they are unattached to the four marks are they called conceptual characteristics.
Speaking again to Śūnyatā-jāti (Subhūti): one should seek the true vision by means of all [conventional] views. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "At the time of seeing the seer, the seer..."
It is not seeing. Even seeing is already free from seeing; seeing cannot reach it. This is what is called true seeing.

Subhūti, if there were someone who took seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and used them for giving as a gift, and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who had resolved upon bodhicitta and upheld this sutra—even [a single verse]...
To receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain even as little as four lines of verse for others brings merit far superior to that.
How does one explain it for others? Without grasping at appearances, remaining unmoving in suchness.
When the sutra reached this point, it spoke again of giving. After awakening, the Bodhisattva does not accept merit.

To uphold the verses of the sutra and expound them for others is exceptionally sublime; it is merely the exposition of the wondrous meaning, rather than the ordinary names, phrases, or sentences comparable to those who interpret the meaning based solely on the literal text.
This refers to expounding upon True Suchness (Tathatā) without grasping at external phenomena.
The characteristics of speech and written words do not stir from the nature of the Middle Way, suchness (*tathatā*).

To be able to expound the Buddha-mind and continue the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom is called "expounding" (*yan*). Where speech and silence are one and the same, there is no dharma that can be spoken;
yet, it is spoken with fervent constancy—this is called "speaking" (*shuo*). When the sutra reaches this point, all speech and written words are themselves reality.
Illusion. That which is illusion is itself reality. The Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Therefore, a verse is spoken to conclude [the discussion]. Why is this so?
All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning—thus should one contemplate them.
Why is this? The Buddha himself elucidated it, saying: "For what reason do you preach for the sake of others?
Do not grasp at signs; remain as suchness, unmoving. He then spoke in verse: "All Buddha-dharmas are conditioned dharmas; they are false and unreal..."
In reality, it is like a dream: existing while one sleeps, but entirely non-existent after waking. It is like a magical illusion:
existing through illusory arts, but lacking true reality. It is like a bubble: appearing to exist on the outside, but being truly empty within. It is like a shadow:
existing in dependence upon light, and vanishing when the light ceases. It is like dew: existing in dependence upon grass, and disappearing as soon as it is seen. Like...
As for lightning, it exists before the thunder but does not exist after it; thus, such contemplation is not true.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely devoid of a real characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). This entire True Scripture is contained within the true characteristic of Suchness (*tathatā*).
To speak of existence or non-existence is, in every case, mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all the world— including gods, humans, and asuras— having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly filled with joy.
"Believing, accepting, and practicing.
This is the standard formula for concluding a sūtra. As for the phrase "all were greatly rejoiced," it means that they have perfectly harmonized with [the teaching] in their hearts;
they believe it truly and accept it earnestly, practicing it without fail.
The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra
